earth-orbit-satellites.name: Earth-orbit satellites
earth-orbit-satellites.description: Small uncrewed satellites: the first step into orbit, and the first test of what space does to living things.

one-crew-capsules.name: One-person capsules
one-crew-capsules.description: Capsules for a single pilot: the first flights to carry a person into space and bring them home.

lunar-probes.name: Lunar probes
lunar-probes.description: Uncrewed craft sent to the Moon: to fly past it, strike it, circle it, land on it and bring back its soil.

sun-probes.name: Sun probes
sun-probes.description: Spacecraft in their own orbits around the Sun, measuring the solar wind and the magnetic fields it carries.

mercury-probes.name: Mercury probes
mercury-probes.description: A probe to the innermost planet, reached by swinging past Venus on the way in.

venus-probes.name: Venus probes
venus-probes.description: Craft for the planet hidden under clouds: flybys, orbiters with radar, and landers built to find out what lies beneath.

mars-probes.name: Mars probes
mars-probes.description: Flybys, orbiters and landers for the red planet, launched when Earth and Mars line up about every two years.

jupiter-probes.name: Jupiter probes
jupiter-probes.description: The first craft to cross the asteroid belt and fly through the radiation around the largest planet.

saturn-probes.name: Saturn probes
saturn-probes.description: A probe bent onto a path to Saturn by Jupiter's gravity, for the first close look at the rings.

space-planes.name: Space planes
space-planes.description: Winged craft that fly to the edge of space and land on a runway, carried aloft by an aircraft or launched on a rocket.

two-crew-capsules.name: Two-crew capsules
two-crew-capsules.description: Capsules for two or three people, built to learn what a trip to the Moon needs: long flights, spacewalks, rendezvous and docking.

lunar-expeditions.name: Lunar expeditions
lunar-expeditions.description: Crewed flights to the Moon: around it, into orbit about it, and down to its surface and back.

three-crew-capsules.name: Three-crew capsules
three-crew-capsules.description: The lunar spacecraft proved in Earth orbit first: long flights, spacewalks, and their landers flown and docked close to home.

sputnik-1.name: Sputnik 1
sputnik-1.description: The simplest satellite that could still make history: a polished sphere with a radio transmitter that anyone with a receiver can hear. Fly it to show the world your agency can reach orbit.
sputnik-1.historyNote: Sputnik 1 was a stopgap. Korolev's bureau was building a much heavier science satellite, Object D, but it was running late and the R-7 was falling short of its planned performance. Korolev pushed for PS-1 instead, short for 'simplest satellite', and it was built in a few months. Object D flew the following May, as Sputnik 3.
sputnik-1.longDescription: The first artificial satellite, launched on 4 October 1957 by an R-7, the Soviet intercontinental missile. The satellite was kept as simple as possible: no science package, only a radio and sensors for its own temperature and pressure. The hard part was the rocket, which had to reach nearly 8 km/s, the speed at which a falling object keeps missing the Earth. Its orbit ran from about 215 to 939 km, once every 96 minutes, and its two frequencies near 20 and 40 MHz let amateurs track it. It fell back on 4 January 1958 after about 1,440 orbits.

sputnik-2.name: Sputnik 2
sputnik-2.description: A heavier satellite with a sealed cabin for a passenger: the first animal in orbit. There is no way to bring the passenger home.
sputnik-2.historyNote: Sputnik 2 was ordered in time for the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution, which left the engineers about four weeks. Its passenger, a stray dog named Laika, could not come home. For decades the official story was that she lived for days in orbit. In 2002 a Russian scientist revealed that her cabin had overheated and she died within hours of launch.
sputnik-2.longDescription: The first flight to carry an animal into orbit, launched on 3 November 1957. Nobody knew how a body would cope with the launch and then with weightlessness, and Sputnik 2 was the test: its telemetry sent the dog's pulse, breathing and blood pressure to the ground. It also carried two spectrophotometers for the Sun's ultraviolet and X-rays, and a cosmic-ray counter. Its orbit reached about 1,660 km at its highest. It stayed up 162 days and burned up on 14 April 1958. A craft that could bring an animal back was the next step: Vostok.

korabl-sputnik-2.name: Korabl-Sputnik 2
korabl-sputnik-2.description: A Vostok capsule flown without a pilot, carrying two dogs, mice, rats and plants, and bringing them all back. It proves the capsule can keep living things alive in orbit and return them safely.
korabl-sputnik-2.historyNote: In August 1960 the dogs Belka and Strelka became the first animals to orbit the Earth and come back alive, after about a day in space. Strelka later had puppies. Khrushchev gave one of them, Pushinka, to Caroline Kennedy, and Pushinka went on to raise puppies of her own at the White House.
korabl-sputnik-2.longDescription: The first flight to prove that the Vostok capsule could keep living things alive in orbit and bring them home. It launched on 19 August 1960 with the dogs Belka and Strelka, 40 mice, two rats and plants, and came down the next day after about 25 hours. A television camera watched the dogs throughout. The flight had to prove the whole chain: life support, retrofire, reentry and parachutes. The dogs rode in a cabin that was ejected from the capsule and landed under its own parachute, as a cosmonaut would. The attempt before, on 28 July, had killed two dogs when the rocket broke up. On 12 April 1961 Gagarin flew a Vostok.

vostok.name: Vostok
vostok.description: A ball-shaped capsule for one cosmonaut, flown mostly by its automatics. It can make short hops or stay in orbit for days, and its pilot leaves by ejection seat before landing.
vostok.historyNote: On 12 April 1961, Vostok 1 carried Yuri Gagarin once around the Earth in 108 minutes. He did not land in the capsule: he ejected at about 7 km and came down under his own parachute. Soviet officials kept that quiet for years, because the rules for an official flight record required the pilot to land with his craft.
vostok.longDescription: Vostok was built by Sergei Korolev's OKB-1 to put a person in orbit as soon as possible. Since nobody knew how a human would cope with weightlessness, the ball-shaped craft could fly the whole mission without its pilot, whose manual controls were locked, the code in a sealed envelope. Its orbit was low enough to decay within about ten days, and it carried supplies for that long, in case the retrorocket failed. Dogs flew it first, then six cosmonauts from 1961 to 1963, among them Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space. Each left the capsule by ejection seat before landing.

explorer-1.name: Explorer 1
explorer-1.description: A small, light satellite packed with instruments instead of mass: a cosmic-ray counter, temperature sensors and a micrometeorite detector. What it measures matters as much as reaching orbit.
explorer-1.historyNote: America's first planned satellite was the Navy's Vanguard, picked because it wasn't a missile program. After Sputnik, the first Vanguard attempt, shown on television in December 1957, rose a little over a meter and exploded. The Army's rocket team under Wernher von Braun, with JPL building the satellite, had Explorer 1 in orbit within two months, on 31 January 1958.
explorer-1.longDescription: America's first satellite, launched from Cape Canaveral on the night of 31 January 1958 on a Juno I: an Army Jupiter-C missile topped by three stages of small solid rockets. Those stages rode in a tub spun up before launch: the guided first stage aimed the stack, and the spin kept the unguided stages above it steady. James Van Allen's Geiger counter, built to count cosmic rays, made the flight a scientific one. Its orbit, which ran from about 358 to 2,550 km, would carry the counter far above the sounding rockets that had measured cosmic rays before, and nobody knew what it would find there.

mercury.name: Project Mercury
mercury.description: America's first crewed spacecraft: a cone-shaped capsule for one astronaut, flown first on short suborbital hops, then in orbit. Unlike Vostok, the astronaut stays aboard and splashes down at sea.
mercury.historyNote: During John Glenn's orbital flight in February 1962, a sensor suggested that Friendship 7's heat shield had come loose. Mission Control told him to keep the retrorocket pack strapped on through reentry, in the hope that its straps would hold the shield in place. He came home safely. The warning turned out to come from a faulty switch.
mercury.longDescription: Project Mercury, approved on 7 October 1958, had three goals: put a person in orbit, find out whether he could work there, and bring him and the capsule back safely. Nobody knew whether a pilot could swallow, see or think clearly while weightless, so the capsule could fly itself, and chimpanzees went first: Ham on a suborbital hop on 31 January 1961, Enos twice around the Earth that November. Short Redstone flights came before Atlas orbits, and six astronauts flew between 1961 and 1963, the last for 34 hours and 22 orbits. Each stayed in his capsule all the way down to a splashdown at sea.

pegasus.name: Pegasus
pegasus.description: A satellite with huge folding panels that count the specks of dust that hit them, to show how often a spacecraft would be struck by micrometeoroids.
pegasus.historyNote: Three Pegasus satellites flew in 1965 on Saturn I rockets. Their detector wings spanned about 29 meters and rode up folded inside a dummy Apollo service module. Engineers feared micrometeoroids could puncture an Apollo spacecraft's skin; Pegasus counted the hits so designers knew what they were up against.
pegasus.longDescription: Three large targets for counting dust in orbit, flown on Saturn I rockets in 1965. The grains they counted weighed between about a ten-millionth and a ten-thousandth of a gram, but they strike at many kilometers a second, and nobody knew how often one would get through a thin wall. Each Pegasus carried about 200 square meters of detector panels in three thicknesses, from 0.04 to 0.4 mm of aluminum, so the counts gave a curve of hits against skin thickness. The satellites reported until 1968; the first two stayed in orbit until 1978 and 1979.

biosatellite.name: Biosatellite
biosatellite.description: A recoverable capsule carrying plants, insects and other small organisms, to study how living things grow and change in weightlessness.
biosatellite.historyNote: Biosatellite II came home in 1967 after 45 hours, about a day early, because a tropical storm threatened the recovery area; an aircraft caught its capsule. Biosatellite III carried a macaque named Bonny on a flight planned for 30 days. After about nine days he stopped eating and drinking, NASA brought him down early, and he died soon after.
biosatellite.longDescription: NASA's series of recoverable satellites for biology, run by its Ames Research Center, with General Electric building the craft. Six flights were planned and three flew, on Delta rockets, from 1966 to 1969. The question was whether weightlessness changes how living things grow and how they respond to radiation, and only a matched comparison could answer it: identical specimens stayed on the ground as controls. Biosatellite II carried a strontium-85 source that exposed some specimens to gamma rays in orbit. The specimens had to come home quickly to be studied, so the recovery mattered as much as the flight.

orbiting-frog-otolith.name: Orbiting Frog Otolith
orbiting-frog-otolith.description: A small satellite carrying two frogs wired up to record the organs of balance in their inner ears, to learn how weightlessness confuses the sense of up and down.
orbiting-frog-otolith.historyNote: NASA launched the Orbiting Frog Otolith on 9 November 1970 on a Scout rocket. Electrodes in the two bullfrogs' balance nerves recorded how the inner ear coped with weightlessness, and with spells of artificial gravity from a small centrifuge, for almost a week. The frogs were never meant to come back.
orbiting-frog-otolith.longDescription: A NASA biology satellite that asked whether the balance organs of the inner ear adapt to weightlessness. The otolith organs sense gravity through tiny crystals resting on sensory hair cells. With nothing pulling the crystals down, they send signals the brain cannot use, a suspected cause of space sickness. The experiment came from Torquato Gualtierotti at NASA's Ames Research Center and was first meant to ride on an Apollo flight. In orbit the frogs' responses changed at first and came back toward normal in the last day or so, a hint that the system adjusts.

pioneer-4.name: Pioneer 4
pioneer-4.description: A small probe sent past the Moon and on into orbit around the Sun, the first American craft to escape the Earth's gravity.
pioneer-4.historyNote: Pioneer 4, launched on 3 March 1959 on a Juno II, was the first American spacecraft to escape the Earth's gravity. Its second stage burned too long, so it passed about 60,000 km from the Moon, too far for its sensor to trigger. It sent data for 82 hours and still circles the Sun.
pioneer-4.longDescription: The Army and JPL's second try at the Moon. Pioneer 3 had fallen back in December 1958 from about 102,000 km, about 1,000 km/h short of escape speed, after its first stage shut down a few seconds early. Pioneer 4 flew on the same Juno II: a Jupiter missile with clusters of small solid rockets on top, which together had to reach more than 11 km/s. It became the first American craft to escape the Earth and orbit the Sun. On the way out its counters measured the radiation around the Earth and beyond. Tracking stations followed it to about 655,000 km, a record at the time.

zond-5.name: Zond 5
zond-5.description: An uncrewed lunar capsule with living passengers aboard, flown around the Moon and brought home through the atmosphere at lunar return speed.
zond-5.historyNote: In September 1968 Zond 5 carried two steppe tortoises, fruit fly eggs and plants around the Moon and splashed down in the Indian Ocean, where Soviet ships recovered it. The tortoises were the first vertebrates to go around the Moon and come home. Apollo 8 took the first people there three months later.
zond-5.longDescription: The 7K-L1 was the Soviet craft meant to fly two cosmonauts around the Moon and straight home, with no stop in lunar orbit. Earlier attempts had failed. Zond 5, in September 1968, was the first craft to go around the Moon and come back, with living things aboard, passing about 1,950 km above the far side. It tested the navigation and the Proton rocket with its Blok D stage, but the hardest part was the return: a capsule coming back from the Moon meets the air at about 11 km/s, and must enter at an angle neither too steep to survive nor too shallow to stay in. After Apollo 8 the crewed flight lost its point and was cancelled.

ranger-3.name: Ranger 3
ranger-3.description: A probe aimed straight at the Moon, taking pictures all the way down until it strikes the surface.
ranger-3.historyNote: Ranger 3 launched in January 1962. A guidance fault gave it too much speed: it reached the Moon 14 hours early and missed it by about 37,000 km. Its television camera and its seismometer capsule, meant to survive the crash and keep reporting, never got to work.
ranger-3.longDescription: The first of three Rangers meant to hit the Moon with two jobs at once: television pictures all the way down, and a seismometer set on the surface to listen for moonquakes. It asked a great deal of 1962 technology: an Atlas-Agena B to throw 330 kg toward the Moon, an aim good enough to hit it, and a capsule that a small rocket would slow just before the crash. A gamma-ray spectrometer rode along too, and made the first measurements of gamma rays between the planets. Rangers 3, 4 and 5 all failed, and the later Rangers carried cameras alone.

luna-2.name: Luna 2
luna-2.description: A probe aimed to hit the Moon: the first human-made object to reach another world.
luna-2.historyNote: On 13 September 1959 Luna 2 struck the Moon east of Mare Imbrium, the first human-made object to reach another world. It carried two balls of small metal pentagons bearing the Soviet coat of arms, built to scatter on impact. Khrushchev gave a copy to President Eisenhower.
luna-2.longDescription: The second Soviet try at hitting the Moon, after Luna 1 missed by about 6,000 km in January 1959. Launched on 12 September 1959, it flew a direct path and struck at about 3.3 km/s some 38 hours later, the first human-made object to reach another world. On the way it released a cloud of sodium vapor that observatories could photograph, to show where it was. Its magnetometers found no lunar magnetic field within their sensitivity, and its ion traps made one of the first direct measurements of the solar wind. Jodrell Bank in England tracked it, which helped convince doubters in the West that it had arrived.

pioneer-2.name: Pioneer 2
pioneer-2.description: An early lunar orbiter, small enough for the rockets of its day, with a camera and instruments for radiation and magnetism.
pioneer-2.historyNote: Pioneer 2 never got far. It launched on 8 November 1958, but its Thor-Able's third stage failed to light, probably because of a broken wire, and it climbed to about 1,550 km before falling back 42 minutes later. Its instruments still sent back data on the way up and down.
pioneer-2.longDescription: The third of the Able probes, built by Space Technology Laboratories and launched for NASA on 8 November 1958 on a Thor-Able. The plan asked for something no one had done: send a probe toward the Moon, then 2.6 days later fire a solid rocket at exactly the right moment to brake into lunar orbit, at a time when no rocket had yet reached escape speed. Its instruments covered radiation, magnetism, micrometeoroids and temperature, with a television scanner for the Moon's face. None of the three Able lunar probes got near the Moon. The next American probes, Pioneer 3 and 4, flew on the Army's Juno II.

lunar-orbiter.name: Lunar Orbiter
lunar-orbiter.description: A camera platform in lunar orbit that develops its own film on board and scans the pictures for radio, to map landing sites.
lunar-orbiter.historyNote: Five Lunar Orbiters flew in 1966 and 1967 to photograph possible Apollo landing sites, and all five worked. Each developed its film on board, scanned it and radioed the pictures home. When their work was done, each was deliberately crashed into the Moon.
lunar-orbiter.longDescription: Five orbiters, flown in 1966 and 1967, to find where Apollo could land safely. Apollo's planners needed to see craters and boulders far smaller than any telescope on Earth could show. The first three flew low orbits near the equator and photographed 20 candidate landing sites. Each developed its film on board and scanned it for radio. The last two went into high polar orbits and mapped almost the whole Moon. Controllers tracked every orbit closely, since Apollo would have to fly the same paths.

surveyor.name: Surveyor
surveyor.description: A three-legged robot lander that brakes with a rocket and settles softly onto the Moon, to prove the ground can carry a spacecraft.
surveyor.historyNote: Surveyor 3 landed in April 1967. In November 1969 Apollo 12 set down less than 200 meters away, and Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over and brought back its television camera and other parts, so engineers could see what more than two years on the Moon had done to them.
surveyor.longDescription: Seven robot landers launched by Atlas-Centaur from 1966 to 1968, to learn whether the Moon's surface would bear a spacecraft or swallow it in dust. Five landed. Surveyor 1, on 2 June 1966, was the first American soft landing, four months after the Soviet Luna 9. With no crew, the craft had to measure its own height and speed by radar and throttle its engines all the way down. Later Surveyors dug trenches with a scoop and measured the soil's chemistry with an alpha-scattering instrument, and everything they learned went to Apollo's planners.

luna-15.name: Luna 15
luna-15.description: A robot lander with a drill and a small return rocket, meant to scoop up lunar soil and fly it back to Earth.
luna-15.historyNote: Luna 15 was the last Soviet chance to bring lunar soil home before Apollo 11. It was still in lunar orbit when Armstrong and Aldrin landed, and it crashed in Mare Crisium on 21 July 1969 while they were on the surface. A robot sample return finally succeeded with Luna 16 in 1970.
luna-15.longDescription: The Ye-8-5 was a robot built to do what Apollo did with people: land, collect lunar soil and fly it home. Luna 15 left Earth on 13 July 1969, three days before Apollo 11, and entered lunar orbit on 17 July. Controllers spent days checking its systems and adjusting its orbit before trying to land: with no pilot aboard, the landing radar would have to judge the ground alone. It began its descent after 52 orbits. The design itself worked: Luna 16, 20 and 24 later brought soil home.

luna-3.name: Luna 3
luna-3.description: A probe that swings behind the Moon and photographs the side that never faces the Earth.
luna-3.historyNote: On 7 October 1959 Luna 3 took 29 photographs of the far side of the Moon in about 40 minutes, developed the film on board, and later scanned 17 of them for radio. Rough as they were, they showed mountainous ground quite unlike the side we see.
luna-3.longDescription: Luna 3 was sent to photograph the side of the Moon that never faces the Earth, and its path did most of the work. It carried no engine to correct its course, so the launch alone had to aim it past the Moon's south pole at about 6,200 km and around behind it. The Moon's gravity then bent its orbit so that it came back over the northern hemisphere, where the Soviet tracking stations stood. It had to prove that a probe could photograph a target, process the pictures itself and send them home across hundreds of thousands of kilometers.

luna-17.name: Luna 17
luna-17.description: A lander that lowers ramps and sends a remote-controlled rover out to drive across the Moon.
luna-17.historyNote: Lunokhod 1 rolled down Luna 17's ramps on 17 November 1970. Built to last three lunar days, it worked through eleven and drove about 10.5 km, steered by drivers on Earth through a delay of several seconds. Its operations ended on 4 October 1971, the anniversary of Sputnik 1.
luna-17.longDescription: Luna 17 carried the first rover to the Moon, Lunokhod 1, launched on 10 November 1970 to land in Mare Imbrium, the Sea of Rains. The hard part was driving at all: a crew on Earth steered from television pictures that arrived seconds late, so every move was planned from the last frames, with one operator driving and another keeping the rover's main antenna pointed at the Earth. The rover had to survive each two-week lunar night on its own heat and wake up again. Its months of driving and soil tests showed what a machine driven from Earth could do on another world.

pioneer-sun-orbiter.name: Pioneer Sun orbiter
pioneer-sun-orbiter.description: Spin-stabilized probes placed in their own orbits around the Sun, to measure the solar wind and space weather between the planets.
pioneer-sun-orbiter.historyNote: Pioneer 6 was launched in December 1965 to watch the solar wind from its own orbit around the Sun. It far outlived its design: on 8 December 2000 controllers made contact once more, 35 years after launch, the last time anyone heard from it.
pioneer-sun-orbiter.longDescription: The Pioneer Sun orbiters were small probes sent into orbits around the Sun close to the Earth's own, to measure the solar wind, magnetic fields and cosmic rays between the planets. Pioneer 6, the first, circled the Sun between about 0.81 and 0.99 times the Earth's distance, once every 311 days, so over the years it drifted around to the far side of the Sun. That was the point: spread out along the Earth's orbit, the probes sampled space at widely separated places at once. In November 1968 Pioneer 6 became the first spacecraft tracked as it passed behind the Sun, its radio signal probing the Sun's outer atmosphere on the way.

mariner-10.name: Mariner 10
mariner-10.description: A probe that uses Venus's gravity to fall inward to Mercury: the first flight to use one planet to reach another.
mariner-10.historyNote: Mariner 10 flew past Venus on 5 February 1974, the first spacecraft to use one planet's gravity to reach another. The flyby bent its path inward, and it passed Mercury three times in 1974 and 1975, the first time at 703 km. The technique had been worked out on paper decades before.
mariner-10.longDescription: Mariner 10 was sent to Mercury, which is hard to reach because a probe falling toward the Sun gathers speed it must not keep: a direct flight would have needed a bigger, costlier rocket. Instead it left on an Atlas-Centaur on 3 November 1973 for Venus, whose gravity bent its path inward. Giuseppe Colombo of the University of Padua saw that the probe's resulting orbit around the Sun, 176 days long, was exactly two of Mercury's years, so it could meet the planet again and again. Each pass found the same half in sunlight, so a little under half of Mercury was mapped: a cratered, Moon-like world with a weak magnetic field.

mariner-5.name: Mariner 5
mariner-5.description: A flyby probe passing close to Venus, studying its atmosphere with radio signals that skim through it.
mariner-5.historyNote: Mariner 5 flew past Venus on 19 October 1967, a day after the Soviet Venera 4 dropped a capsule into its atmosphere. Scientists from both countries published the two missions' results together, a rare joint effort in the middle of the space race.
mariner-5.longDescription: Mariner 5 was NASA's second look at Venus, almost five years after Mariner 2. It carried no camera, since Venus's clouds hide the ground. Its main tool was its own radio. Launched on 14 June 1967, the probe passed behind the planet as seen from the Earth, and its signal sank through deeper and deeper air and bent, and from the bending scientists worked out how the atmosphere's density and temperature change with height. Its ultraviolet photometer found a halo of hydrogen around the planet, and it found no magnetic field.

pioneer-venus-orbiter.name: Pioneer Venus Orbiter
pioneer-venus-orbiter.description: An orbiter that maps Venus's surface through the clouds by radar and watches its upper atmosphere for years.
pioneer-venus-orbiter.historyNote: Pioneer Venus 1 reached Venus in December 1978 and kept working for almost 14 years. Its radar mapped 93 % of the band from 74 degrees north to 63 degrees south, the first map of nearly the whole hidden surface. When its fuel ran out its orbit sank, and on 8 October 1992 it burned up in the atmosphere it had studied.
pioneer-venus-orbiter.longDescription: The Pioneer Venus Orbiter was NASA's first spacecraft to circle Venus. Launched on 20 May 1978, it was braked into orbit on 4 December by a solid rocket motor. Its orbit was a long ellipse lasting about a day, dipping to roughly 150 km at its low point, so on every pass it sampled the upper air and ionosphere directly while its radar measured the ground below. It found a planet smoother than the Earth, with almost no magnetic field, clouds of sulfuric acid and frequent lightning, and its highest peak, Maxwell Montes, about 11 km above the average surface.

venera-15.name: Venera 15
venera-15.description: An orbiter with a large side-looking radar, mapping Venus's northern hemisphere in detail.
venera-15.historyNote: Venera 15 reached Venus in October 1983, with its twin Venera 16. Their side-looking radars mapped the northern hemisphere from the pole to about 30 degrees north, and American and Soviet scientists later turned the data into joint maps.
venera-15.longDescription: Venera 15 and its twin Venera 16 tackled a problem cameras cannot solve: the surface of Venus lies under permanent cloud, and from orbit only radar sees through it. A radar looking straight down measures height but cannot tell features on either side apart, so these orbiters looked off to one side, about 10 degrees from the vertical, and built pictures from the timing and frequency of the echoes, while an altimeter alongside measured height. Their long orbits, about a day each, came lowest at roughly 1,000 km near 62 degrees north, which is why their maps covered the far north.

pioneer-venus-multiprobe.name: Pioneer Venus Multiprobe
pioneer-venus-multiprobe.description: A carrier that releases one large and three small probes, which fall through Venus's atmosphere at widely spaced points and radio back what they find.
pioneer-venus-multiprobe.historyNote: On 9 December 1978 one large and three small probes, named North, Day and Night, fell into Venus's atmosphere. None was built to survive hitting the ground, but two did, and the Day probe kept sending temperatures from the surface for 67 minutes until its batteries ran out.
pioneer-venus-multiprobe.longDescription: The Pioneer Venus Multiprobe was built to sample Venus's atmosphere in several places at once, since one probe can only show one column of air. A single spinning carrier, launched on 8 August 1978, released the large probe on 16 November and the three small ones four days later, each on its own path to a different target: the day side, the night side and the high north. In December they all fell in. The large probe slowed under a parachute and the small ones fell without one. Below about 50 km all four found almost the same temperatures, though they were thousands of kilometers apart.

venera-7.name: Venera 7
venera-7.description: A heavily armored lander built to reach the surface of Venus and send data home from it.
venera-7.historyNote: On 15 December 1970 Venera 7's parachute failed and it hit Venus at about 60 km/h, coming to rest on its side. Controllers thought it had died, but weeks later the recordings showed a faint signal: it had kept reporting from the ground for some 23 minutes, the first data from the surface of another planet.
venera-7.longDescription: Venera 7 was the next Soviet attempt to reach the surface of Venus and keep working there, after three earlier probes had fallen silent on the way down. Launched on 17 August 1970, it had to settle what radio and radar from the Earth could only hint at: how hot and how dense the bottom of Venus's atmosphere really is. It measured the temperature, and from that and models of the air scientists worked out the pressure. It kept sending a faint signal for about 20 minutes from the ground: the first transmission from the surface of another planet. Its lessons shaped the landers that followed.

venera-lander.name: Venera lander
venera-lander.description: A carrier craft and a lander travel together to Venus; the lander dives to the surface while the carrier relays its signal.
venera-lander.historyNote: Venera 9 landed on 22 October 1975 and sent back the first picture ever taken on the surface of another planet: jagged rocks on a layer of dust. A lens cap stayed on, so only half the planned view came through. The lander lasted about 53 minutes, and its carrier became the first spacecraft to orbit Venus.
venera-lander.longDescription: The Venera landers of the mid-1970s, beginning with Venera 9 and 10 in 1975, were a new and much heavier design, launched on the Proton rocket. Each mission paired a lander with a carrier that braked into orbit around Venus or, on later missions, flew past it, and relayed the lander's signal to the Earth. The relay solved an old problem: a lander lying on the ground can hardly aim a radio at the Earth. These missions had to show that a lander could last long enough on the surface to take pictures of it.

mariner-6.name: Mariner 6
mariner-6.description: A flyby probe passing close over Mars and photographing its surface and atmosphere.
mariner-6.historyNote: Mariner 6 flew past Mars on 31 July 1969, about 3,430 km up, and sent back 75 pictures. They showed so many craters that the camera team called Mars more like the Moon than the Earth. Its pictures of the south polar cap were intriguing enough that controllers reprogrammed its twin, Mariner 7, in flight to take more of them.
mariner-6.longDescription: Mariner 6 and its twin Mariner 7 were the second American look at Mars, four years after Mariner 4. Launched on 25 February 1969, they were the first Mariners to ride an Atlas-Centaur, whose extra power let them carry a much heavier set of instruments: two cameras, infrared and ultraviolet spectrometers and an infrared radiometer on a pointable platform. Mariner 6 passed south of the equator. Besides its pictures, it found an atmosphere of about 98 % carbon dioxide at a pressure of 6 to 7 millibars, well under 1 % of the Earth's, and a polar cap that looked like frozen carbon dioxide.

mariner-9.name: Mariner 9
mariner-9.description: The first spacecraft to orbit another planet, mapping Mars from pole to pole.
mariner-9.historyNote: Mariner 9 reached Mars on 14 November 1971, the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, and found it hidden by a planet-wide dust storm. Only Olympus Mons and three other volcanoes showed above the haze. JPL put the mapping off until the dust settled, and Mariner 9 went on to map most of Mars.
mariner-9.longDescription: Mariner 9 was built to do what a flyby could not: stay at Mars for months and map it. That meant braking into orbit on arrival, with an engine burn of just over 15 minutes, five and a half months after its launch on 30 May 1971. Its orbit, about 12 hours long, was later trimmed so that its passes fitted the schedule of the Goldstone tracking station that received its pictures. Over almost a year it sent 7,329 pictures and mapped about 85 % of the planet at 1 to 2 km, finding the great canyon Valles Marineris, about 20 volcanoes and channels that looked as if flowing water had cut them.

viking.name: Viking
viking.description: An orbiter and a lander: the orbiter surveys Mars and picks the site, the lander searches the soil for signs of life.
viking.historyNote: Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976. Its Labeled Release experiment fed soil samples nutrients laced with radioactive carbon and watched for gas, and the first result looked positive. Other tests found no organic molecules, and most scientists blame reactive chemicals in the soil, but the experiment's designer maintained it had found life.
viking.longDescription: Viking was NASA's attempt to land on Mars and look for life, with two identical missions launched in August and September 1975 on Titan-Centaur rockets. Each orbiter and lander flew to Mars joined, and the orbiter examined the planned landing site from orbit before letting the lander go. That step mattered: Viking 1's first site turned out to be strewn with boulders, so its landing was put off from 4 July while a safer spot was found farther west in Chryse Planitia. The landers then worked for years, Viking 1 until November 1982, while the orbiters mapped the planet and relayed the landers' data.

mars-2.name: Mars 2
mars-2.description: An orbiter carrying a lander, which carries a small rover on skis to step across the surface.
mars-2.historyNote: After the Mars 2 lander crashed, Mars 3 made the first soft landing on Mars on 2 December 1971, in the middle of a planet-wide dust storm. It began sending a picture and fell silent within seconds. Its small rover, meant to walk on two skis at the end of a 15-meter cable, never left the lander.
mars-2.longDescription: Mars 2 was the Soviet attempt of 1971 to put a craft in orbit around Mars and a lander on its surface in one mission. Launched on a Proton on 19 May 1971, nine days before its twin Mars 3, it parted the two only on arrival, so the orbiter could relay the lander's signals home. The lander even carried a small rover, to step across the ground on skis. Landing meant solving three problems at once: air too thin for parachutes alone, a surface no one had seen up close, and radio delays too long to steer from Earth. Between them the two orbiters sent back about 60 pictures and measured surface temperatures from about -110 °C to 13 °C.

mars-m69.name: Mars M-69
mars-m69.description: A heavy Mars orbiter designed for the new Proton rocket, with cameras and instruments to study the planet from orbit.
mars-m69.historyNote: Both Mars M-69 orbiters were lost in 1969, on 27 March and 2 April, when their Proton rockets failed. The project was already late and overweight, and its lander had been dropped from the design before launch.
mars-m69.longDescription: Mars M-69 was meant to give the Soviet Union the upper hand in the 1969 Mars launch window, when NASA was sending Mariner 6 and 7 past the planet. The new Proton could lift a far heavier probe than the rockets behind earlier Soviet planetary craft, so the plan was an orbiter on a long ellipse, swinging from about 1,000 km to about 70,000 km above Mars, mapping it with cameras and about ten other instruments. The design began as a conversion of the Luna E-8 landing stage, which proved unsuited to a six-month cruise. After the losses, Lavochkin reworked the design into the M-71: Mars 2 and Mars 3.

pioneer-10.name: Pioneer 10
pioneer-10.description: A probe sent through the asteroid belt to Jupiter, and on out of the Solar System.
pioneer-10.historyNote: Pioneer 10, launched on 2 March 1972, was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and to fly past Jupiter, on 4 December 1973. It carries a plaque showing where the Earth is, in case anyone ever finds it. Its last signal reached Earth in 2003.
pioneer-10.longDescription: Pioneer 10 was sent to answer two questions before anything bigger was risked: could a spacecraft cross the asteroid belt, and could it live through Jupiter's radiation? Leaving Earth at about 51,700 km/h, faster than anything before it, it entered the belt in July 1972 and came out in February 1973 having met far fewer particles than feared. At Jupiter it passed about 130,000 km above the cloud tops and took about 500 pictures, though the radiation set off false commands and cost it a planned image of Io. It then headed out of the Solar System, and in June 1983 it became the first human-made object beyond Neptune's orbit.

pioneer-11.name: Pioneer 11
pioneer-11.description: A probe that flies past Jupiter and uses its gravity to swing across to Saturn.
pioneer-11.historyNote: Pioneer 11 flew past Jupiter in 1974, and Jupiter's gravity swung it onto a path to Saturn, which it reached in 1979, the first spacecraft there. In 1995 its power ran too low to work its instruments.
pioneer-11.longDescription: Pioneer 11, launched on 6 April 1973, followed its twin to Jupiter and was steered far closer. On 3 December 1974 it passed about 42,500 km above the cloud tops at about 171,000 km/h; the speed kept its time in the radiation belts short, and its steep path returned the first pictures of Jupiter's polar regions. Jupiter's gravity then bent its course back across the Solar System, a trip of almost five years, with two course corrections on the way. At Saturn it took about 440 images, and its crossing of the planet's bow shock, 1.5 million km out, gave the first sure evidence that Saturn has a magnetic field.

x-15.name: X-15
x-15.description: A rocket plane dropped from under the wing of a bomber, flying faster and higher than any aircraft before it, to the edge of space and back to a dry lakebed.
x-15.historyNote: Three X-15s made 199 flights between 1959 and 1968, carried aloft under the wing of a B-52. Joe Walker flew one to 354,200 feet, about 108 km, in August 1963, and in 1967 Pete Knight reached Mach 6.7, about 4,520 mph, in the modified X-15A-2.
x-15.longDescription: The X-15 was built to find out what happens to an aircraft, and its pilot, at speeds and heights nobody had reached: heating from the air, control where the air is too thin for wings and rudders, and the return from the edge of space to a landing. A B-52 carried it to about 13,700 m and let it go; the pilot fired its engine for 80 to 120 seconds, then glided home without power to a dry lakebed. Twelve pilots flew it, and eight of them went above 80 km, high enough for American astronaut wings. Its data on heating, reaction controls and pilots under stress fed into Mercury, Gemini, Apollo and the Space Shuttle.

mig-e-154.name: OKB-MiG E-154
mig-e-154.description: A rocket plane from the MiG design bureau, carried up under the belly of a bomber and dropped, to fly faster and higher than any Soviet aircraft before it, to the edge of space and back to a runway.
mig-e-154.historyNote: The E-154 is our own invention, the Soviet answer to the X-15, in place of a rocket-launched space plane in the game that inspired this one. The real Mikoyan bureau did design a Soviet space plane, Spiral, but only its subsonic test craft, the MiG-105, was built. It made eight flights between 1976 and 1978.
mig-e-154.longDescription: The E-154 is the Soviet answer to the X-15: a rocket plane from the Mikoyan bureau, carried aloft under a bomber, dropped, flown on rocket power to the fringe of space, and glided back to a runway. Its flights have to prove what the X-15 did: that its structure survives hypersonic heating, that a pilot can keep control with thrusters where wings no longer bite, and that a glide from that height can end on a chosen strip. The bureau's real height record came from a jet: in 1977 a modified MiG-25, the E-266M, zoomed to 37,650 m, still the record for an aircraft that takes off under its own power.

gemini.name: Gemini
gemini.description: A two-person capsule built to master what a Moon landing needs: long flights, spacewalks, and rendezvous and docking with another craft.
gemini.historyNote: Gemini 8 made the first docking of two spacecraft, with an Agena, in March 1966. Soon after, a thruster on the capsule stuck and set the pair rolling. Neil Armstrong and David Scott undocked, the capsule spun up to a turn a second, and Armstrong stopped it with the reentry thrusters, which forced an early landing in the Pacific.
gemini.longDescription: Gemini was there to learn, in Earth orbit, the skills a Moon landing would need, before Apollo had to use them. NASA set its goals in January 1962: flights of up to two weeks, rendezvous and docking with another craft, work outside the spacecraft, and reentry to a chosen spot. Ten two-person flights in 1965 and 1966 met nearly all of them. Gemini 7 stayed up almost 14 days, longer than a trip to the Moon and back. Crews learned that closing on another craft means thinking in orbits, since thrusting straight at a target raises the chaser's orbit and drops it behind, and spacewalkers found how hard it is to work in a pressure suit.

circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.name: Circumlunar Gemini: Earth-orbit tests
circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.description: Tests close to home for a Gemini sent around the Moon: a heat shield for lunar return speed, and the Transtage that would push it there.
circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.
circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.longDescription: These are tests that never flew: what a circumlunar Gemini would have had to prove close to Earth first. A capsule back from the Moon meets the air at about 11 km/s instead of about 7.8, carrying roughly twice the energy per kilogram, so it needed a thicker heat shield, and a 1964 NASA study found the extra mass too much for a plain Titan II. The other half was the push: dock a Gemini to a Transtage launched separately, then fire the stage with the capsule riding on its front. Gemini 10 and 11, carried higher by their docked Agenas, came closest to trying the idea.

lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.name: Lunar-orbit Gemini: Earth-orbit tests
lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.description: Tests in Earth orbit for a Gemini that could brake into lunar orbit: its heat shield and the propulsion module behind it.
lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.
lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.longDescription: A Gemini that stops in lunar orbit, rather than looping around and falling home, needs a burn of nearly 1 km/s to brake into orbit and about as much again to leave, judging by Apollo's later burns. That takes an engine which fires on time after days in space, with the crew's only way home depending on it, and a heat shield for the fast return. These Earth-orbit tests, never flown, would have proven the propulsion module behind the capsule: starting it after long cold waits, and steering a Gemini with a heavy stage attached. In a NASA study of July 1964 the role went to an Agena, sent toward the Moon with the capsule by a Centaur.

gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.name: Gemini Direct Ascent: Earth-orbit tests
gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.description: Tests in Earth orbit for a Gemini that would land on the Moon in one piece, and its landing and ascent modules.
gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.
gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.longDescription: Direct ascent means landing the whole spacecraft, return fuel and capsule included, and then launching all of it back off the Moon. Every kilogram landed must first be braked down and then lifted up again, which is why NASA chose lunar orbit rendezvous for Apollo in 1962: a small lander leaves the heavy return craft in orbit. A Gemini version, launched whole on a single heavy rocket, was one of the last direct-ascent studies. It never flew. Tests in Earth orbit would have had to prove its stages: a hydrogen engine that restarts after days of coasting, a landing stage that can set the stack down gently, and an ascent stage that cannot fail.

voskhod.name: Voskhod
voskhod.description: The Vostok capsule rebuilt to carry two or three people, and fitted with an inflatable airlock for the first spacewalk.
voskhod.historyNote: Voskhod 1 flew three cosmonauts in October 1964, the first crew of more than one, with no spacesuits: there was no room for them. On Voskhod 2 in March 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, 12 minutes on a 5.35 m tether. His suit ballooned in the vacuum, and he had to let air out of it to squeeze back into the airlock.
voskhod.longDescription: Voskhod was a quick way to beat Gemini to a crew of more than one: rather than wait for a new craft, Korolev's bureau rebuilt Vostok to carry more people and, in a second version, to let one of them step outside through an inflatable airlock. Removing the ejection seat made the room, but it also took away the crew's only escape on the pad or during launch. Voskhod 1 carried three men for about a day from 12 October 1964. On Voskhod 2 in March 1965 the automatic retrofire failed, the crew fired the engine by hand on a later orbit, and they came down far off course in dense forest in the Perm region. Later flights were cancelled.

soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.name: Soyuz 7K-L1: Earth-orbit tests
soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.description: The stripped-down Soyuz meant to carry two cosmonauts around the Moon, first tested in flights close to Earth.
soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.historyNote: The 7K-L1 flew without a crew under the name Zond. In September 1968 Zond 5 went around the Moon and came home with two tortoises aboard, and Apollo 8 carried people around it three months later. No 7K-L1 ever flew a crew.
soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.longDescription: The 7K-L1 was a Soyuz cut down to carry two cosmonauts once around the Moon and home, launched by the Proton with a Blok D upper stage. Before that, the pieces had to prove themselves near Earth: the Proton itself, the Blok D's restart in orbit, and the craft's star sensors and gyroscopes for finding its way in deep space. The first test, Kosmos 146, flew on 10 March 1967 on the Proton-K's first launch, and went well. A month later Kosmos 154 was stranded in low orbit: a control fault dropped the small motors that settle the Blok D's propellant before ignition, and its main engine never lit.

soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.name: Soyuz 7K-L3: Earth-orbit tests
soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.description: The lunar-orbit Soyuz and its one-person LK lander, tested in Earth orbit before any trip to the Moon.
soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.historyNote: The LK lander was tested without a crew in Earth orbit three times, as Kosmos 379, 398 and 434 in 1970 and 1971, firing its engine as if landing on the Moon and lifting off again. The last test qualified it as flightworthy. It never went to the Moon: the N1 rocket meant to carry it never made a successful flight.
soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.longDescription: Before a cosmonaut could be left alone on the Moon, every step of the landing had to work in Earth orbit first, where a failure still had a quick way home. The lunar complex was two craft: the Soyuz 7K-LOK, which would wait in lunar orbit, and the LK lander. Tests had to prove that the two could find each other and dock with no tunnel between them, that a cosmonaut in a lunar suit could spacewalk from one to the other, and that the Blok D stage could brake into orbit and lower the lander. In December 1970 Kosmos 382 fired a Blok D three times in Earth orbit to rehearse those burns.

lk-700-earth-orbit.name: LK-700: Earth-orbit tests
lk-700-earth-orbit.description: A heavy direct-ascent lunar craft, tested in long flights around the Earth before it heads for the Moon.
lk-700-earth-orbit.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei proposed the LK-700 in 1964 as a simpler path than Korolev's: one craft on his giant UR-700, landing directly on the Moon and returning with no rendezvous. The money went to the N1 instead, the UR-700 was never built, and the LK-700 was cancelled in 1974.
lk-700-earth-orbit.longDescription: The LK-700 was never built, so its Earth-orbit flights are a plan, not a record. Chelomei's scheme put the whole expedition on one UR-700 launch: about 150 t in low orbit, of which some 17 t would reach the Moon's surface and only a capsule of about 3 t would come home. Before anyone trusted it, a crew of two had to live aboard for the length of a lunar trip, about eight days, and its landing and return stages had to start, stop and restart in vacuum. One thing Earth orbit could not prove: the capsule's return from the Moon at about 11 km/s.

gemini-eor-earth-orbit.name: Gemini EOR: Earth-orbit tests
gemini-eor-earth-orbit.description: A light lunar lander for Gemini, assembled in Earth orbit, put through its paces close to home.
gemini-eor-earth-orbit.historyNote: In 1961 Langley engineers sketched the smallest Moon lander anyone took seriously: one astronaut standing on an open rocket platform with landing legs, good for two to four hours on the surface. Gemini's manager, James Chamberlin, later built a plan to land Gemini crews on the Moon around a lander much like it. NASA chose Apollo instead.
gemini-eor-earth-orbit.longDescription: Earth-orbit rendezvous meant building the Moon ship in orbit from pieces launched separately, so the pieces had to be shown to find each other and lock together long before anyone trusted the method far from home. Gemini itself took the first steps: Gemini 6A and 7 met in orbit in December 1965, and Gemini 8 made the first docking, with an Agena, on 16 March 1966. These test flights go further: the service module joined to the capsule, the tug's engine restarted on command, and the open lander flown and recovered while home is still a single orbit away.

circumlunar-gemini.name: Circumlunar Gemini
circumlunar-gemini.description: A Gemini capsule pushed around the Moon by a Transtage stage it docks with in Earth orbit.
circumlunar-gemini.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.
circumlunar-gemini.longDescription: A Gemini launched on its Titan II would meet a Transtage, the upper stage of the Air Force's Titan III, dock with it in Earth orbit and ride its burn onto a path that swings around the Moon and falls back to Earth with no further firing needed. Finding and docking with a stage was work Gemini already did. The hard part was coming home: a capsule returning from the Moon meets the air at about 11 km/s instead of under 8 km/s, with roughly twice the energy to shed per kilogram, and NASA's studies called for a thicker heat shield. Such plans were studied from 1961 to 1965 and never funded.

lunar-orbital-gemini.name: Lunar-orbit Gemini
lunar-orbital-gemini.description: A Gemini capsule with a propulsion module strong enough to brake into lunar orbit and break out again.
lunar-orbital-gemini.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.
lunar-orbital-gemini.longDescription: Flying around the Moon needs one big burn; stopping there needs two more. A lunar-orbit Gemini would carry a propulsion module to brake into orbit around the Moon and later to fire it home again, each burn worth about 900 m/s or more. Both burns come behind the Moon, cut off from Earth's radio, so the crew and the ground learn whether the engine worked only when the craft reappears on the right path. One study had a Centaur send the stack toward the Moon and an Agena make both lunar burns. The prize was a long look at the surface and practice for a landing. It remained a proposal.

gemini-direct-ascent.name: Gemini Direct Ascent
gemini-direct-ascent.description: One large spacecraft built around Gemini that flies straight to the Moon, lands, and lifts off for home.
gemini-direct-ascent.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.
gemini-direct-ascent.longDescription: Direct ascent is the simplest Moon plan to describe and the hardest to launch: one craft goes all the way down to the surface and all the way back. Everything needed for the trip home, the return engine, its propellant and the heat-shielded capsule, has to be landed and then lifted off again, and every kilogram of it costs several more in propellant below it. The Gemini design stacked a braking module with a hydrogen-burning RL10 engine, dropped about 1,800 m above the surface, a landing module, a module for the liftoff and the burn home, and a capsule strengthened for the faster return. It needed a giant rocket to itself.

apollo.name: Apollo
apollo.description: A command and service module with a separate lunar module: two astronauts land while the third waits in lunar orbit, and they meet again to fly home.
apollo.historyNote: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins waited in orbit. Six Apollo missions landed in all, and twelve astronauts walked on the Moon.
apollo.longDescription: Apollo reached the Moon by splitting the job. Two astronauts went down in the lunar module, built for nothing but landing and lifting off, while the third waited in lunar orbit in the command module, which carried the heat shield. Propellant for the trip home never had to be landed and lifted again, and that saving let one Saturn V carry the whole expedition. The price was a rendezvous around the Moon, 384,000 km from home. NASA chose lunar orbit rendezvous in July 1962, over a giant direct-ascent rocket and over assembly in Earth orbit. Crews flew to the Moon from December 1968 to December 1972.

gemini-eor.name: Gemini EOR
gemini-eor.description: A Moon landing assembled from parts launched separately and joined in Earth orbit, with a light open lander for the final step down.
gemini-eor.historyNote: In 1961 Langley engineers sketched the smallest Moon lander anyone took seriously: one astronaut standing on an open rocket platform with landing legs, good for two to four hours on the surface. Gemini's manager, James Chamberlin, later built a plan to land Gemini crews on the Moon around a lander much like it. NASA chose Apollo instead.
gemini-eor.longDescription: Instead of one giant rocket, Earth-orbit rendezvous used several smaller launches: the capsule, a service module, the open lander and a Saturn S-IVB stage as a tug, joined in orbit before the tug pushed the stack toward the Moon. Each launch was easier, but they all had to fly on schedule, because a stage waiting in orbit slowly loses its liquid hydrogen as it boils away. At the Moon the light lander takes a single suited astronaut down to the surface and back up to the waiting stack, with no cabin around him. NASA weighed Earth-orbit rendezvous for Apollo and chose lunar orbit rendezvous in 1962.

soyuz-7k-l1.name: Soyuz 7K-L1 circumlunar
soyuz-7k-l1.description: A two-person Soyuz flown once around the Moon and straight back, without stopping in lunar orbit.
soyuz-7k-l1.historyNote: The 7K-L1 flew without a crew under the name Zond. In September 1968 Zond 5 went around the Moon and came home with two tortoises aboard, and Apollo 8 carried people around it three months later. No 7K-L1 ever flew a crew.
soyuz-7k-l1.longDescription: The 7K-L1 was a Soyuz stripped for one job: a loop around the Moon and back. The orbital module was left off, so two cosmonauts would have shared about 4 m³ for a trip of about a week. A Proton rocket launched it and a Blok D stage sent it toward the Moon on a path that falls back to Earth by itself. Coming home at nearly escape speed, the capsule dipped into the atmosphere, skipped back out and entered again, which spread the braking and let it land in the Soviet Union. Of its uncrewed flights as Zond, only Zond 7 in August 1969 came home in a way that would have been safe for a crew.

soyuz-7k-l3.name: Soyuz 7K-L3 lunar landing
soyuz-7k-l3.description: A lunar-orbit Soyuz and the one-person LK lander: a single cosmonaut goes down while the other stays in orbit.
soyuz-7k-l3.historyNote: The LK lander was tested without a crew in Earth orbit three times, as Kosmos 379, 398 and 434 in 1970 and 1971, firing its engine as if landing on the Moon and lifting off again. The last test qualified it as flightworthy. It never went to the Moon: the N1 rocket meant to carry it never made a successful flight.
soyuz-7k-l3.longDescription: The Soviet landing plan was lunar orbit rendezvous cut to the minimum: two cosmonauts, one of whom goes down. In lunar orbit one cosmonaut would spacewalk from the Soyuz 7K-LOK to the LK, since no tunnel joined the two craft, and land alone after the Blok D stage had done most of the braking. After a short stay he would lift off, dock with the waiting LOK and spacewalk back carrying his samples. Every step had to work without a second pair of hands, and the cosmonaut in orbit could not go down to help. The whole complex rode one N1 rocket, and the program was cancelled in May 1974.

lk-700.name: LK-700 Direct Ascent
lk-700.description: A heavy spacecraft that flies straight to the Moon, lands with its whole crew and returns, launched on the giant UR-700.
lk-700.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei proposed the LK-700 in 1964 as a simpler path than Korolev's: one craft on his giant UR-700, landing directly on the Moon and returning with no rendezvous. The money went to the N1 instead, the UR-700 was never built, and the LK-700 was cancelled in 1974.
lk-700.longDescription: Chelomei's answer to Korolev's lunar orbit rendezvous was to avoid a rendezvous altogether. One UR-700 would put about 150 t in Earth orbit, and stage after stage would burn it down: three clustered stages to leave Earth orbit, a braking stage, a landing stage, and a return stage that lifts off from the Moon with a capsule of about 3 t. Two cosmonauts would land together, stay up to a day and walk on the surface twice, about eight days for the whole trip. The price of skipping the rendezvous was size: a rocket far bigger than any yet built, to put two people on the Moon.

apollo-earth-orbit.name: Apollo: Earth-orbit tests
apollo-earth-orbit.description: The Apollo spacecraft proved close to home: long flights, spacewalks, and the lunar module flown, separated and docked again in Earth orbit.
apollo-earth-orbit.historyNote: Apollo 9 tested the lunar module in Earth orbit in March 1969. With two crewed craft flying at once, the crew named them Spider and Gumdrop. James McDivitt and Russell Schweickart flew Spider away from Gumdrop and back, proving the lander before it went to the Moon.
apollo-earth-orbit.longDescription: Apollo's hardware flew in Earth orbit first, where a crew in trouble could be home within hours instead of days. On 22 January 1968 Apollo 5 flew a lunar module with nobody aboard and fired its ascent engine while it was still joined to the descent stage, as an aborted landing would. In October 1968 Apollo 7 kept three astronauts in the command and service module for nearly 11 days, as long as a lunar trip, and fired the service engine eight times. Only after both did a crew fly the lander away from the command ship and back, with a spacewalk on the same flight.

soyuz-7k-ok.name: Soyuz 7K-OK
soyuz-7k-ok.description: The Earth-orbit Soyuz: long flights, and automatic rendezvous and docking guided by the Igla radar system.
soyuz-7k-ok.historyNote: In October 1967 Kosmos 186 and 188 made the first automatic docking, steered by the Igla system with nobody aboard. In January 1969 Soyuz 4 and 5 made the first docking of two crewed craft, and Aleksei Yeliseyev and Yevgeny Khrunov spacewalked across, since there was no tunnel between the ships.
soyuz-7k-ok.longDescription: The 7K-OK was the first Soyuz, built to practice in Earth orbit what the Moon flights would need: maneuvering, rendezvous, automatic docking guided by the Igla radar system, and long stays. It started badly. Soyuz 1 killed Vladimir Komarov in April 1967 when its parachute failed, and in October 1968 Soyuz 3 reached its uncrewed target but could not dock. In October 1969 Soyuz 6, 7 and 8 put seven cosmonauts in orbit at once, and Soyuz 6 tried welding in vacuum. In June 1970 Soyuz 9 stayed up nearly 18 days, and its crew could barely walk afterward: an early warning for the space station flights that followed.

sputnik-1-satellite.name: Sputnik 1 satellite
sputnik-1-satellite.description: A polished aluminum sphere about half a meter across, with four long antennas and a battery-powered transmitter.
sputnik-1-satellite.historyNote: Sputnik 1 only sent a simple beep, for about three weeks until its batteries ran down. Two physicists at Johns Hopkins' Applied Physics Laboratory found they could work out its whole orbit from the Doppler shift of that beep. Their lab then turned the idea around: if you know a satellite's orbit, the same shift tells you where you are. That became Transit, the US Navy's satellite navigation system, an ancestor of GPS.
sputnik-1-satellite.longDescription: A sphere 58 cm across and 83.6 kg, made of two aluminum alloy hemispheres 2 mm thick, bolted together over a seal, with a polished outer layer against the Sun's heat. Inside, in dry nitrogen, 51 kg of silver-zinc batteries surrounded a 1 W transmitter. A fan switched on above 36 °C, and the length of each beep carried the temperature and pressure. Two pairs of whip antennas, 2.4 and 2.9 m long, trailed back from the front.

sputnik-2-satellite.name: Sputnik 2 satellite
sputnik-2-satellite.description: A sealed, air-conditioned cabin for one dog, with instruments for radiation and sunlight. It stays attached to the rocket's core stage in orbit.
sputnik-2-satellite.historyNote: Sputnik 2's Geiger counter, built by Sergei Vernov's team in Moscow, recorded strange swings in its counts, and the team blamed a small solar flare. Its highest point was over the southern hemisphere, out of reach of the Soviet ground stations, and an Australian team that picked up its signals there had no code to read them.
sputnik-2-satellite.longDescription: A cone about 4 m tall and 2 m across at the base, of about 500 kg, never meant to separate from the core stage of its R-7. The solar instruments rode in the nose. Other compartments held the radios, telemetry and air system, and a sealed, padded cabin held the dog, harnessed, fed with gelatin, wired for her vital signs and watched by a television camera at 10 frames a second. A chemical regenerator absorbed carbon dioxide and gave off oxygen.

vostok-capsule.name: Vostok capsule
vostok-capsule.description: A steel sphere for the cosmonaut, joined to an equipment module with batteries, oxygen and a single retrorocket that can't be restarted.
vostok-capsule.historyNote: Why a ball? A sphere whose weight sits slightly off-center settles heat-shield-first into the air on its own, like a weighted toy that rights itself. So Vostok needed no thrusters to hold its attitude during reentry. The price was a steep, uncontrolled descent: cosmonauts felt around eight times their own weight on the way down.
vostok-capsule.longDescription: A descent sphere 2.3 m across and about 2.4 t, covered all over in heat shield, holding the pilot's ejection seat. Behind it sat a double-cone equipment module of about 2.3 t with batteries, gas bottles and the TDU-1 retrorocket, which gave about 16 kN for some 45 seconds. After the burn the module was cast off. At about 7 km the cosmonaut ejected and came down under a separate parachute, since the sphere landed too hard for a person.

explorer-1-satellite.name: Explorer 1 satellite
explorer-1-satellite.description: A slim cylinder of about 14 kg carrying a Geiger counter, temperature sensors and a micrometeorite detector.
explorer-1-satellite.historyNote: Explorer 1 was meant to spin like a bullet around its long axis. After its first orbit it was tumbling end over end instead. Its flexing wire antennas were bleeding off energy, and a spinning body that loses energy drifts toward spinning around its fattest axis. The surprise taught engineers a rule that every spacecraft designer has followed since.
explorer-1-satellite.longDescription: A slim tube 203 cm long and 15 cm across that stayed fixed to the burnt-out last rocket stage and spun with it. It weighed about 14 kg, 8.3 kg of it instruments: a Geiger counter, five temperature sensors and two micrometeorite detectors, a microphone listening for impacts and a grid of fine wires that broke when hit. Mercury batteries, about 40 % of the payload, ran a 60 mW transmitter for 31 days and a 10 mW one for 105.

mercury-capsule.name: Mercury capsule
mercury-capsule.description: A small cone for one astronaut, with an escape tower on top, a heat shield at the base and a pack of retrorockets strapped over it.
mercury-capsule.historyNote: The first Mercury capsules had two small portholes and a side hatch held by 70 bolts, and the astronaut was meant to climb out through the nose. The astronauts pushed for a real window above their heads and a hatch they could blow off with explosive charges. Both arrived with Liberty Bell 7, the second crewed capsule.
mercury-capsule.longDescription: A cone about 3.3 m tall and 1.9 m across the base, holding one astronaut in pure oxygen at about 0.38 bar. The heaviest flight version weighed about 1.4 tonnes. An escape tower could pull it off a failing rocket, hydrogen peroxide thrusters turned it, and three solid retrorockets in a pack over the heat shield slowed it for reentry. The fiberglass shield, charring away to carry off the heat, then dropped on a skirt that filled with air to cushion the splashdown.

r7-sputnik.name: R-7 (Sputnik)
r7-sputnik.description: The world's first intercontinental missile, adapted to carry a satellite: a core stage ringed by four strap-on boosters, all lit on the launch pad.
r7-sputnik.historyNote: Why light every engine on the ground? In the early 1950s nobody knew whether a large rocket engine could be started reliably high up, in thin air or in vacuum. The R-7's designers sidestepped the question: the core and all four boosters ignite on the pad, and the empty boosters simply fall away. Its descendant, Soyuz, still flies this way.

r7-vostok.name: R-7 (Vostok)
r7-vostok.description: The R-7 with a small upper stage on top, enough to put a crewed Vostok capsule into orbit.
r7-vostok.historyNote: Gagarin's rocket was the R-7 with a third stage, the Block E. Semyon Kosberg's bureau, which had built engines for aircraft, developed its engine in about nine months for the first Moon probes. Three of the first lunar launches failed, and on 2 January 1959 the stage worked for the first time, sending Luna 1 past the Moon. Gagarin rode an improved version of it.

jupiter-c.name: Jupiter-C
jupiter-c.description: A lengthened Redstone missile topped with a spinning cluster of small solid rockets, just enough to put a very light satellite into orbit.
jupiter-c.historyNote: In September 1956 this rocket could have put a satellite in orbit, a year before Sputnik. Washington wanted the first American satellite to come from the civilian Vanguard project, so the Army flew with a dummy top stage filled with sand, and the payload only arced 5,300 km downrange. After Sputnik and a Vanguard exploding on its pad, a Jupiter-C finally launched Explorer 1 in January 1958.

redstone.name: Redstone
redstone.description: A single-stage missile, made safe enough to carry an astronaut. It can only lob a capsule on a short suborbital hop.
redstone.historyNote: Mercury-Redstone 1, in November 1960, became known as the "four-inch flight": the rocket rose about ten centimeters and shut itself down, because a plug had come out in the wrong order and told it the flight was over. The capsule then fired its escape tower away on its own and released its parachutes, leaving a fully fueled rocket on the pad with parachutes draped down its side.

atlas.name: Atlas
atlas.description: A missile built so light that it needs the pressure in its tanks to keep its shape, and powerful enough to put a Mercury capsule into orbit.
atlas.historyNote: The Atlas's steel skin was thinner than a coin, so the rocket had to stay pressurized even on the ground, or it would buckle under its own weight. Like the R-7, it lit all its engines at liftoff, because nobody was sure an engine would start in space. Partway up it simply dropped its two outer engines and flew on with the one in the middle.

pegasus-satellite.name: Pegasus satellite
pegasus-satellite.description: Two long wings of thin detector panels that unfold in orbit, each panel recording the hits of tiny particles.
pegasus-satellite.historyNote: Pegasus answered a question Apollo's designers couldn't answer on the ground: how often would tiny meteoroids punch through a thin spacecraft skin? Its detector panels, and sample shields mounted on them, found far fewer penetrating hits than the worst fears. Engineers could trust the thin-skinned service module and the heat-shield cocoon of the command module.
pegasus-satellite.longDescription: A satellite of about 1,450 kg, fixed to the rocket's spent upper stage, with two long wings, about 4.3 m wide, that unfolded in orbit. Each wing panel was a capacitor: a sheet of aluminum over a thin plastic film on a layer of copper, held charged. A grain that punched through the aluminum briefly shorted the layers, the panel recharged, and the hit was counted. Solar cells powered it, and a television camera watched the wings open.

biosatellite-satellite.name: Biosatellite capsule
biosatellite-satellite.description: A capsule with life support for its small passengers, and a heat shield and parachute to bring them home for study.
biosatellite-satellite.historyNote: Biosatellite 1 carried more than ten million small living things into orbit in December 1966: insects, frog eggs, bacteria, plants. Its capsule separated on schedule, but its small deorbit rocket never fired. The capsule stayed in orbit with its specimens and its data, and it was never recovered.
biosatellite-satellite.longDescription: A spacecraft in three sections: an adapter that stayed in orbit, a reentry vehicle with a small retrorocket and a bowl-shaped heat shield, and inside it the sealed capsule with the specimens and their life support. To come home, the reentry vehicle fired its retrorocket and fell behind its shield. Then the capsule opened its parachute and radioed its position, and an Air Force aircraft caught it in mid-air over the Pacific before it reached the sea.

ofo-satellite.name: OFO satellite
ofo-satellite.description: A small satellite with a water-filled centrifuge for two frogs, wired to record their balance organs.
ofo-satellite.historyNote: The Orbiting Frog Otolith flew bullfrogs because their balance organs are very like ours. Fine electrodes recorded single nerve fibers from the inner-ear sensors that feel gravity, and the frogs rode in water, which cushioned them from the launch. The satellite was built to keep every acceleration below a thousandth of the Earth's gravity.
ofo-satellite.longDescription: A cylinder about 0.76 m across and 1.2 m long, of about 133 kg. After launch it let out weights on cables to stop its spin and extended four booms, whose extra inertia kept it steady. Inside, a sealed 41 kg canister held the frogs in a water-filled centrifuge that swung their heads to 0.6 g for 14 seconds at a time. A silicone-rubber artificial lung, an oxygen bottle and a carbon dioxide absorber kept the water fresh at about 16 °C.

pioneer-4-probe.name: Pioneer 4 probe
pioneer-4-probe.description: A light cone carrying radiation counters, spun for stability and fired on a path past the Moon.
pioneer-4-probe.historyNote: Pioneer 4 weighed about 6 kg: a cone of fiberglass half a meter tall, washed with gold so it would conduct electricity and act as part of the antenna. The white stripes painted on it were its whole thermal control, meant to keep the inside between 10 and 50 degrees Celsius. A ring of mercury batteries powered it.
pioneer-4-probe.longDescription: A cone about 51 cm tall and 23 cm wide at the base, riding on the Juno II's last stage and spun for stability. Two Geiger-Mueller tubes counted radiation, and a photoelectric sensor was meant to see the Moon's light at close range and trigger a test of a lunar photography system. About 11 hours into the flight a despin mechanism slowed it from 480 to about 11 turns a minute.

zond-5-probe.name: Zond 5 spacecraft
zond-5-probe.description: An uncrewed Soyuz 7K-L1 with a descent capsule and life support for its animal passengers.
zond-5-probe.historyNote: Zond 5's trip home went wrong. Its star tracker, fogged by gas from its own heated interior coating, delayed a course correction, and on the way back the capsule could not fly its planned guided reentry. It fell ballistically, at much higher g-forces than planned, into the Indian Ocean instead of Kazakhstan. The tortoises inside survived.
zond-5-probe.longDescription: A Soyuz without its orbital module, of about 5.4 t: a service module with the main engine and solar panels, and the bell-shaped descent capsule, with a cone and a dish antenna for deep space in the orbital module's place. It gained a gyro platform and star sensors, lost its reserve parachute, and carried life support for animals. The capsule was meant to dip into the atmosphere, climb back out and dive in again, splitting its braking into two gentler passes.

ranger-3-probe.name: Ranger 3 probe
ranger-3-probe.description: A probe with a television camera and a capsule meant to survive the impact and keep reporting.
ranger-3-probe.historyNote: Rangers 3 to 6 were baked before launch to kill any Earth microbes that might contaminate the Moon. The engineer running the sterilization warned that the heat was damaging the electronics, and NASA's board of inquiry agreed after the failures. Later Rangers were built with parts that were never baked, and Ranger 7 sent back over 4,000 pictures in 1964.
ranger-3-probe.longDescription: A hexagonal base 1.5 m across carrying a dish antenna and two solar panels spanning 5.2 m, with a television camera and its telescope looking ahead. On top sat the 42.6 kg capsule: a seismometer, a transmitter and batteries for 30 days, in a casing of balsa wood. A radar altimeter was to release it about 21 km above the surface and fire a retrorocket beneath it, so it would hit slowly enough to bounce, roll and keep working.

luna-2-probe.name: Luna 2 probe
luna-2-probe.description: A sphere of instruments and pennants bearing the Soviet emblem, built to strike the Moon.
luna-2-probe.historyNote: Luna 2 was not the only thing from Earth to hit the Moon that day. The rocket's last stage, which had pushed the probe onto its path, followed it across the same 38 hours and struck about half an hour after it, somewhere no one recorded. Luna 2 itself was much like Luna 1, which had missed the Moon in January and become the first craft to orbit the Sun.
luna-2-probe.longDescription: A sphere of about 390 kg with whip antennas, carrying magnetometers, Geiger and scintillation counters, ion traps to catch charged particles, and a radio. It also carried the pennants bearing the Soviet emblem. It had no engine of its own, so the rocket's last stage had to set it on a path that would hit the Moon unaided.

pioneer-2-probe.name: Pioneer 2 probe
pioneer-2-probe.description: A small probe with a kick motor of its own to brake into lunar orbit.
pioneer-2-probe.historyNote: Pioneer 1 and 2 were short cylinders with a cone at each end, built around a solid rocket that was meant to brake them into orbit around the Moon. Eight small rockets on the upper cone would trim their speed on the way. Each carried a scanning infrared camera, meant to take crude pictures of the Moon's surface.
pioneer-2-probe.longDescription: A probe about 74 cm across and 76 cm long, of about 39 kg, built around a Thiokol TX-8-6 solid motor meant to slow it into orbit around the Moon. Its instruments were an ion chamber, a magnetometer, a micrometeoroid sensor, a counter telescope for cosmic rays and temperature sensors, all running on batteries. The motor gave a single fixed push: the probe had to arrive on the right path to use it.

lunar-orbiter-probe.name: Lunar Orbiter spacecraft
lunar-orbiter-probe.description: A camera with a small film laboratory on board, solar panels, and an engine for lunar orbit.
