lunar-orbiter-probe.historyNote: On 23 August 1966 Lunar Orbiter 1 pointed its camera past the Moon's edge and photographed the Earth from about 380,000 km, the first picture of our planet from near the Moon. It wasn't on the plan: a fault in the camera's motion compensation had changed the film schedule and left room for a few unplanned frames.
lunar-orbiter-probe.longDescription: A craft of about 387 kg, stabilized on all three axes, with four solar panels, a dish antenna and a rocket engine for braking into lunar orbit. Its 68 kg Kodak camera, adapted from a reconnaissance satellite's, shot through two lenses at once, 610 mm and 80 mm, onto one roll of film. The film was developed on board against a damp Bimat processing web, dried, then read by a fine scanning beam of light and radioed home strip by strip.

surveyor-lander.name: Surveyor lander
surveyor-lander.description: A three-legged lander with a braking rocket, throttleable engines for the last stretch, and a camera.
surveyor-lander.historyNote: On 17 November 1967 Surveyor 6 fired its engines again on the Moon, rose about 4 meters and set down about 2.5 meters away: the first liftoff from another world. The hop let its camera look at its first landing site and judge the soil from a second angle, and it showed that a craft could fire its engines on the Moon.
surveyor-lander.longDescription: A triangular aluminum frame about 3 m tall on three legs with shock absorbers, about 995 kg at launch and about 300 kg on the Moon. A solid retrorocket, over half its launch mass, fired about 75 km up and was dropped at about 11 km. Three throttleable vernier engines, steered by Doppler radar, then brought it down to about 3.4 m above the ground and cut off, letting it drop at about 3 m/s. A television camera on top looked out over the site.

luna-15-probe.name: Luna 15 lander
luna-15-probe.description: A landing stage with a drill arm, and a small ascent rocket carrying a sealed capsule for the sample.
luna-15-probe.historyNote: The Soviet sample-return craft needed no rendezvous and no navigator. After the drill had sealed its core in a small capsule, the ascent stage fired straight up from the lander and flew directly back toward Earth. Luna 16's capsule, in September 1970, plunged ballistically into the atmosphere and came down under a parachute in Kazakhstan.
luna-15-probe.longDescription: A landing stage on four legs, with fuel tanks, a landing radar, a television camera and a drill on an arm, carrying an ascent stage of about 520 kg. The drill could reach about 35 cm and swing its core up into a small spherical capsule on the ascent stage. The ascent stage had its own engine and tanks, and had to reach about 2,700 m/s to head for Earth.

luna-3-probe.name: Luna 3 probe
luna-3-probe.description: A probe with a camera that develops film on board and scans it for radio.
luna-3-probe.historyNote: Luna 3 spun slowly for most of its flight, but for its photographs it had to point. Photocells found the Sun and the Moon, small gas jets turned the craft and held it steady, and a photocell on its upper end started the camera when it saw the sunlit far side. It was the first Soviet spacecraft that could hold itself steady on all three axes.
luna-3-probe.longDescription: A sealed cylinder about 1.3 m long with rounded ends, weighing about 280 kg and filled with gas at about a fifth of sea-level pressure. Solar cells on its skin charged batteries inside, and shutters opened to shed heat when the inside grew warmer than 25 °C. Its camera had two lenses and 35 mm film. After the shoot the film was developed, fixed and dried on board, then read by a moving spot of light and sent home like a fax.

luna-17-lander.name: Luna 17 lander
luna-17-lander.description: A landing stage with folding ramps at each end, for the rover to roll off.
luna-17-lander.historyNote: Luna 17's landing stage carried its rover on top, with folding ramps on two opposite sides, so Lunokhod could drive off whichever way was clear of boulders. It used the east side. The stage itself had a full rocket landing system of its own: a main engine, tanks and four legs, the same design that brought Luna 16's sample drill down two months earlier.
luna-17-lander.longDescription: The landing stage was a squat platform of propellant tanks around a main engine, about 3.3 m across its legs, with the rover carried on top and folding ramps on both sides for it to drive down. Extra tanks used for braking into lunar orbit were dropped there, so the stage did not carry their weight down to the ground. From an orbit 19 by 85 km high it fired its engine and came down in about six minutes. On the surface, rover included, it weighed about 1,800 kg.

lunokhod-1-rover.name: Lunokhod rover
lunokhod-1-rover.description: An eight-wheeled rover under a hinged lid of solar cells, driven from Earth with a few seconds' delay.
lunokhod-1-rover.historyNote: Lunokhod 1 carried a French laser reflector. After the rover fell silent in 1971 nobody knew exactly where it had stopped, and laser beams from Earth found nothing for almost 40 years. In 2010 a NASA orbiter photographed the rover, and within weeks a telescope in New Mexico got a strong reflection back from it on its first try.
lunokhod-1-rover.longDescription: Lunokhod was a pressurized, tub-shaped body about 1.35 m high, riding on eight wheels, each with its own electric motor, so one failed motor would not stop it. A convex lid lined with solar cells opened by day to charge its batteries and closed at night, when a polonium-210 heat source kept the inside warm. Four television cameras showed the way to its drivers on Earth, a ninth wheel measured distance, and instruments tested the soil's strength and chemistry.

pioneer-6-probe.name: Pioneer Sun probe
pioneer-6-probe.description: A small drum-shaped probe covered in solar cells, spinning about once a second to keep stable.
pioneer-6-probe.historyNote: Pioneer 6 and its three sisters, spaced around the Sun along the Earth's orbit, became the first solar weather network in space. They could see parts of the Sun days before its rotation turned them toward the Earth, and their warnings of solar storms went to airlines, power companies and NASA's planners for the Apollo flights.
pioneer-6-probe.longDescription: A drum about 0.94 m across and 0.81 m tall, its sides covered in solar cells that gave about 79 W. It spun about once a second, its axis at right angles to the Earth's orbit, so its instruments swept around the sky with every turn and the spin itself kept it steady. A directional antenna kept contact with the Earth at up to 512 bits a second, and a 1.8 m boom held the magnetometer away from the craft's own magnetic field.

mariner-10-probe.name: Mariner 10 probe
mariner-10-probe.description: A probe with two television cameras and a sunshade, steered past Venus and on to Mercury.
mariner-10-probe.historyNote: Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft to steer with the pressure of sunlight. Its gyroscopes and solar panels had set it wobbling, wasting the nitrogen gas its thrusters needed, so controllers tilted the two panels slightly differently and let sunlight pushing on them hold it steady. The gas ran out on 24 March 1975, eight days after its last pass of Mercury.
mariner-10-probe.longDescription: Mariner 10 was built around an eight-sided magnesium frame about 1.4 m across that held its electronics, with two solar panels each about 2.7 m long reaching out to the sides. A sunshade on the side facing the Sun protected it as it fell to about half the Earth's distance from the Sun. A dish 1.37 m across sent pictures home at up to 117.6 kilobits a second, and a 5.8 m boom held the magnetometers clear of the craft.

mariner-5-probe.name: Mariner 5 probe
mariner-5-probe.description: A flyby probe with instruments that read Venus's atmosphere from the way its radio signal bends.
mariner-5-probe.historyNote: Mariner 5 began as the spare for Mariner 4, the first probe to photograph Mars. When Mariner 4 worked, NASA rebuilt the spare for Venus: it lost its camera, gained a sunshade, and had its solar panels turned to face the other way and made smaller, since it would be flying toward the Sun instead of away.
mariner-5-probe.longDescription: An eight-sided magnesium frame about 1.27 m across, weighing about 245 kg, with four solar panels that spanned 5.5 m and gave about 555 W near Venus, backed by a silver-zinc battery. A dish antenna sat on top, and a mast held the low-gain antenna and the magnetometer. It had no camera. Its instruments measured ultraviolet light, magnetic fields and charged particles, and its radio was itself an instrument, read as the signal passed through the atmosphere.

pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.name: Pioneer Venus Orbiter
pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.description: A drum-shaped orbiter with a radar mapper and instruments for the upper atmosphere.
pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.historyNote: Pioneer Venus 1 found a second career as a comet observatory. In early 1986, when Halley's Comet passed behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, the orbiter at Venus had a clear view. Its ultraviolet spectrometer tracked the hydrogen streaming off the comet and measured how much water it was losing, near the comet's most active time.
pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.longDescription: A squat drum 2.5 m across and 1.2 m high, spinning about five times a minute, with solar cells on its sides that gave about 312 W at Venus. A dish 1.09 m across was turned against the spin so that it stayed pointed at the Earth while the body spun beneath it. A solid rocket motor braked it into orbit. Its radar looked down on the low part of each orbit to measure the height of the ground, building a map with features about 75 km across.

pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.name: Pioneer Venus Multiprobe
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.description: A carrier bus with one large and three small entry probes, each with its own heat shield.
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.historyNote: The bus that carried the four Pioneer Venus probes had no heat shield and no parachute, but it was not wasted. About 90 minutes after the probes went in, it followed them, and its two mass spectrometers sampled the thin upper air that the probes had fallen through too fast to measure. It sent data for about a minute before it burned up near 110 km.
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.longDescription: A spinning drum 2.5 m across, like the orbiter's, carrying four cone-shaped probes. The large probe, about 1.5 m across and some 315 kg, held its instruments in a sealed vessel behind a nose cone and later rode a parachute. The three small probes, about 0.8 m across and 90 kg each, kept their shells all the way down and opened small doors for their instruments about 70 km up.

venera-15-probe.name: Venera 15 orbiter
venera-15-probe.description: An orbiter carrying a large dish for side-looking radar mapping.
venera-15-probe.historyNote: Venera 15 and 16 were built from the orbiter half of the earlier Venera lander missions, with a radar dish about 6 meters long in place of a lander. Because Venus is hidden under its clouds, they mapped it by radar from the side, at a resolution of one to two kilometers, over eight months.
venera-15-probe.longDescription: A heavy orbiter with a long cylindrical body, a curved radar antenna at one end and a smaller dish for the altimeter beside it, aimed at the center of the planet while the radar looked aside. The radar worked at a wavelength of 8 cm, sending pulses down to one side and recording their echoes, and the computers on board stored each picture until it was complete. At launch it weighed about 5,250 kg, of which about 4,000 kg was the craft without its fuel.

venera-7-probe.name: Venera 7 lander
venera-7-probe.description: A small, heavily insulated descent capsule built to reach the surface of Venus whole.
venera-7-probe.historyNote: Venera 7's lander was built far stronger than Venera 4, 5 and 6, which had all fallen silent on the way down, with a titanium hull in place of aluminum and magnesium alloy, and was chilled to about −8 °C by its carrier before entry. The extra strength cost weight, so it carried few instruments.
venera-7-probe.longDescription: The Venera 7 lander was a descent capsule of about 500 kg, built far stronger than the landers before it, wrapped in insulation, with its parachute packed on top. The parachute opened about 60 km up, held small at first by a cord made to melt away lower down, so that the canopy opened fully only in the denser air below. Its temperature sensors were its main instrument: the surface pressure was later worked out from the temperature, not measured.

venera-9-probe.name: Venera lander and carrier
venera-9-probe.description: A carrier that can fly past or orbit Venus, and a lander protected by a spherical shell.
venera-9-probe.historyNote: Venera 9's lander dropped its parachutes about 50 km above Venus, while it was still far from the ground. Below that the air is so thick that a flat metal disc around the lander, about 2 meters across, was brake enough: it came down the rest of the way on the disc alone and touched the ground at about 7 meters per second.
venera-9-probe.longDescription: The carrier had solar panels and its own engine, able to brake into orbit around Venus and relay the lander's signal. The lander rode on top inside a spherical shell 2.4 m across that took the heat of entry at about 10.7 km/s and was then shed. Inside sat a sealed sphere about 80 cm across holding the instruments, wrapped in insulation, with a fluid loop to spread the heat and a crushable ring beneath to soften the landing.

mariner-6-probe.name: Mariner 6 probe
mariner-6-probe.description: A flyby probe with cameras and spectrometers on a turntable platform.
mariner-6-probe.historyNote: Mariner 4 had sent its pictures of Mars home at about 8 bits a second; each picture took hours. Mariner 6 and 7 had a channel for 16,200 bits a second, almost 2,000 times as fast. Together they sent back about 200 pictures in 1969, against Mariner 4's 22 four years earlier.
mariner-6-probe.longDescription: Mariner 6 was built on an eight-sided magnesium frame about 1.38 m across, with four solar panels spanning 5.79 m that gave 449 W at Mars and a 1 m dish antenna on top. Below the frame a platform that turned on two axes pointed its two television cameras, infrared and ultraviolet spectrometers and infrared radiometer. Pictures went first to an analog tape recorder and were played back to the Earth after the flyby.

mariner-9-probe.name: Mariner 9 orbiter
mariner-9-probe.description: An orbiter with a large engine for braking into Mars orbit, and cameras for mapping.
mariner-9-probe.historyNote: Mariner 9 had a twin. Mariner 8 was launched on 8 May 1971, but its Centaur upper stage began to tumble and it fell into the Atlantic. Mariner 9 left three weeks later with a repaired Centaur and both missions' work in its plan: mapping most of the planet, and watching how its surface and air changed over time.
mariner-9-probe.longDescription: Mariner 9 kept the Mariner family's eight-sided frame, but almost half of its launch mass of about 1,000 kg was propellant and gas, feeding a 1,340 N engine that could be restarted up to five times. Four solar panels spanned 6.89 m. A scan platform carried wide- and narrow-angle cameras, an infrared radiometer, an ultraviolet spectrometer and an infrared interferometer spectrometer. It worked until its attitude-control gas ran out.

viking-orbiter.name: Viking orbiter
viking-orbiter.description: An orbiter that carries the lander to Mars, scouts its landing site and relays its signals.
viking-orbiter.historyNote: On 25 July 1976, while it was looking for a landing site for Viking 2, the Viking 1 orbiter photographed a hill in the Cydonia region that looked like a human face, with the Sun low and the shadows making eyes, a nose and a mouth. NASA released it as a curiosity. Higher-resolution pictures in 1998 showed an ordinary eroded hill.
viking-orbiter.longDescription: The Viking orbiter grew out of Mariner 9's design: an eight-sided ring about 2.5 m across, with four wings of solar panels giving 620 W at Mars. Most of its launch mass of 2,328 kg was propellant for a 1,323 N engine that braked the orbiter and lander together into orbit. Cameras, an infrared mapper and a water vapor detector rode on a pointable platform, and a relay radio passed on the lander's data.

viking-lander.name: Viking lander
viking-lander.description: A lander with a sampling arm and a small onboard laboratory to look for signs of life.
viking-lander.historyNote: To keep Earth's microbes off Mars, each Viking lander was sealed in a protective shell and baked whole at about 112 degrees Celsius for some 40 hours, with every part designed to survive it. The shell stayed closed until the spacecraft had left Earth orbit. It was one of the most thorough sterilizations of any spacecraft.
viking-lander.longDescription: The Viking lander had a six-sided aluminum base on three legs, with two plutonium-powered generators under wind screens. It came down inside an aeroshell whose heat shield took the entry, then a parachute about 16 m across opened 6 km up. Three throttling hydrazine engines, each spreading its exhaust through 18 nozzles to disturb the ground less, set it down at about 2.4 m/s. A sampling arm fed soil to the instruments inside.

mars-2-probe.name: Mars 2 spacecraft
mars-2-probe.description: An orbiter with a lander attached, the lander carrying a small rover tethered by a cable.
mars-2-probe.historyNote: Mars 2 and 3 arrived during the biggest dust storm ever seen on Mars, but they could not wait: their computers released the landers on a schedule set before launch, and it couldn't be changed. Mariner 9, arriving at the same time, simply waited in orbit. The Mars 2 lander crashed on 27 November 1971, the first human-made object to reach the surface.
mars-2-probe.longDescription: At launch the craft weighed about 4.65 tonnes: a 3.4 tonne orbiter with a 1.2 tonne descent module on top. Inside a cone-shaped aeroshell 2.9 m wide sat the landing capsule, a sphere 1.2 m across, braked by aeroshell, parachutes and a small rocket, with foam inside to absorb the impact. On the ground four petals would open to set it upright and show its two cameras the view, and an arm would set down the 4.5 kg rover, to walk on skis at the end of its cable.

mars-m69-probe.name: Mars M-69 orbiter
mars-m69-probe.description: A heavy orbiter with cameras, built to make full use of the Proton's lift.
mars-m69-probe.historyNote: The M-69 orbiters weighed about 4.85 tonnes, far more than earlier Soviet planetary probes, and needed the new Proton rocket. Georgy Babakin's team at Lavochkin threw out the planned design and started a new spacecraft only 13 months before launch. Both were lost when their Protons failed, one in the third stage and one about 30 seconds after liftoff.
mars-m69-probe.longDescription: A heavy orbiter, too heavy for any earlier Soviet rocket, meant to make full use of the Proton. Two fixed solar panels of about 7 square meters gave it power, and a 2.8 m dish antenna carried its data home. Its cameras exposed film, about 160 frames in all, which was scanned on board and sent to Earth as a television signal. Its engine had to start in weightlessness, so a set of small tanks of bubble-free propellant fired briefly first to settle the main supply.

pioneer-10-probe.name: Pioneer 10 probe
pioneer-10-probe.description: A probe powered by radioisotope generators, since sunlight is too weak at Jupiter for solar panels.
pioneer-10-probe.historyNote: Sunlight at Jupiter is too weak for solar panels of any practical size, so Pioneer 10 carried four small nuclear generators that turned the heat of decaying plutonium into about 155 watts. They rode on two 3-meter trusses to keep them well away from the instruments, and a third boom held the magnetometer more than 6 meters out.
pioneer-10-probe.longDescription: A spacecraft of about 258 kg built around a 2.74 m dish antenna, with a six-sided equipment compartment behind it. It spun about five times a minute around the dish's axis, which held the dish pointed at Earth the way a spinning top holds its tilt, and a movable feed in the antenna sensed which way Earth lay. An 8 watt transmitter carried its data home. Sunlight at Jupiter is too weak for solar panels, so radioisotope generators, heated by plutonium, powered it.

pioneer-11-probe.name: Pioneer 11 probe
pioneer-11-probe.description: A twin of Pioneer 10, steered through Jupiter's gravity onto a path to Saturn.
pioneer-11-probe.historyNote: At Saturn in September 1979, Pioneer 11 crossed the plane of the rings at the same distance Voyager 2 would have to cross it to go on to Uranus. If the faint outer region held enough ring material to wreck a spacecraft, better to find out with Pioneer. It got through safely, found a new ring, now the F ring, and nearly hit a small, unknown moon.
pioneer-11-probe.longDescription: Built to the same design as Pioneer 10: a spinning craft of about 259 kg with a 2.74 m dish and four radioisotope generators. It added one instrument, a fluxgate magnetometer for the strong fields close to Jupiter. Its own small thrusters made the corrections that steered it through Jupiter's gravity onto a path to Saturn. Its generators gave about 144 watts at Jupiter but only about 100 at Saturn, and that slow fall in power set the length of its working life.

agena-target-vehicle.name: Agena target vehicle
agena-target-vehicle.description: An upper stage with a docking collar and an engine that can restart: a target for docking practice, and once docked, a stage that can push the capsule higher.
agena-target-vehicle.historyNote: On 25 October 1965 Gemini 6's crew sat on the pad waiting for their Agena to reach orbit. It exploded about six minutes after launch, and the flight was scrubbed. Within days NASA had a new plan: launch Gemini 7 on its two-week flight, and use it as Gemini 6's target. In December the two capsules flew in formation, as close as about 30 centimeters.
agena-target-vehicle.longDescription: The Agena was a Lockheed upper stage, about 7.9 m long and 1.5 m across, launched by an Atlas and fitted with a McDonnell docking adapter to take the Gemini's nose. Its main engine burned UDMH with nitric acid for about 71 kN of thrust, and was qualified for up to 15 starts. Once docked, the crew could command it to fire, and twice it carried a Gemini far higher than the capsule could go alone: to about 760 km on Gemini 10, and to a record 1,369 km on Gemini 11.

x-15-aircraft.name: X-15 rocket plane
x-15-aircraft.description: A black, stubby-winged rocket plane with a single rocket engine and small thrusters for control where the air runs out.
x-15-aircraft.historyNote: Above about Mach 5 the air heats a plane's skin to hundreds of degrees, enough to ruin aluminum. The X-15's outer skin was Inconel X, a nickel-chrome alloy, and its structure was designed to soak up the heat of the short, fast flights like a sponge. The pilot sat in an aluminum cabin kept apart from the hot outer shell.
x-15-aircraft.longDescription: About 15 m long, with wings only 6.7 m across, the X-15 weighed about 14 tonnes at launch and under half that with its propellant gone. Its single XLR99 engine burned liquid oxygen and ammonia for up to about 254 kN of thrust, and could be throttled and restarted. Above the air, small hydrogen peroxide thrusters in the nose and wings turned it. Before landing the pilot dropped the lower part of its ventral fin, and the plane touched down on two rear skids and a nose wheel.

mig-e-154-spaceplane.name: MiG E-154 rocket plane
mig-e-154-spaceplane.description: A slender swept-wing rocket plane with a cluster of four rocket engines, a pressurized cockpit, wheels to land on and small thrusters for control above the air.
mig-e-154-spaceplane.historyNote: The real Soviet space plane project, Spiral, planned to launch its orbiter from the back of a hypersonic carrier aircraft: a 52-tonne jet that would climb to almost 30 km at up to six times the speed of sound before releasing it. The carrier was never built, but a subsonic test version of the orbiter flew eight times, the later flights after being dropped from a Tu-95 bomber.
mig-e-154-spaceplane.longDescription: A slender rocket plane with swept wings, a pressurized cockpit and wheeled landing gear for an ordinary runway. Its cluster of four rocket engines follows the pattern of the American XLR11, a four-chamber engine that could not be throttled: the pilot set the thrust by lighting one, two, three or all four. Small gas thrusters would hold its attitude above the air, where its control surfaces have nothing to push against.

voskhod-capsule.name: Voskhod capsule
voskhod-capsule.description: A Vostok sphere with the ejection seat removed to fit more people, a backup retrorocket, and an inflatable airlock.
voskhod-capsule.historyNote: Voskhod was a Vostok with the ejection seat taken out and three couches squeezed in, set crosswise. There was no room for spacesuits, and no way out on the pad or during landing: the crew rode the capsule all the way down, so a small rocket on the parachute lines fired just before touchdown to soften the landing. The crew of Voskhod 1 said they barely felt it.
voskhod-capsule.longDescription: The sphere was Vostok's, about 2.3 m across, with its ejection seat taken out to make room for two or three people. With no seat to ride out on, the crew depended entirely on the capsule's engines, so a backup solid-fuel retrorocket sat on top of the sphere in case the main one failed. For Voskhod 2 an inflatable airlock was fitted to the hatch: stowed, it was only 70 cm wide; extended, it reached 2.5 m long and about 1 m wide inside, and it was thrown away before reentry.

gemini-capsule.name: Gemini capsule
gemini-capsule.description: A two-person capsule with thrusters to change orbit, a radar for rendezvous, and a nose that can dock.
gemini-capsule.historyNote: Gemini was the first crewed spacecraft with a digital computer on board, built by IBM: about 27 kg with 4,096 words of core memory. It worked out the burns for rendezvous, steered during reentry, and stood by as a backup for the Titan rocket's guidance. Mercury had none: its pilots flew with the ground doing the arithmetic.
gemini-capsule.longDescription: An enlarged Mercury on the outside, and the first crewed spacecraft that could change its own orbit. The crew's reentry module sat on an adapter holding the retrorockets, propellant, oxygen, water and power, discarded before reentry. Sixteen thrusters moved it in any direction, a radar in the nose found the target, and the nose could dock. Ejection seats replaced Mercury's escape tower, and a center of gravity set off the axis let the crew steer the reentry by rolling.

gemini-transtage.name: Gemini Transtage
gemini-transtage.description: The Titan's restartable upper stage, docked to a Gemini in orbit to push it toward the Moon.
gemini-transtage.historyNote: The Transtage was the restartable top stage of the Titan III, burning fuels that light on contact so it could be fired again and again. On 16 June 1966 a Titan IIIC used it to place seven small military communications satellites, and a test satellite, into high orbit on a single launch. McDonnell's Moon proposals would have docked a Gemini to one to push it out of Earth orbit.
gemini-transtage.longDescription: The top stage of the Titan III: about 4.6 m tall and 3 m across, about 12 tonnes fully fueled, with two gimbaled engines of about 36 kN each. Its propellants, Aerozine 50 and nitrogen tetroxide, ignite on contact and need no refrigeration, and gas pressure fed them to the engines without pumps, so it could wait in orbit and fire several times, for about 440 seconds in all. A Gemini docked to it would have ridden it out of Earth orbit.

gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.name: Gemini lunar propulsion module
gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.description: A propulsion module behind the capsule, with enough engine to brake into lunar orbit and leave again.
gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.historyNote: Coming home from the Moon means hitting the air at about 11 km/s instead of about 7.8 from Earth orbit, with far more heating. That doomed the simplest lunar Gemini plan: a Centaur stage on a Titan II, good for a 72-hour flight around the Moon, was quickly dropped over worries about Gemini's heat shield. Any lunar Gemini would have needed a new one.
gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.longDescription: A module behind the Gemini capsule, carrying the propellant and a restartable engine for the two big burns at the Moon: into lunar orbit and out again. Its propellants would ignite on contact, so no igniter has to work after days in the cold, and gas pressure rather than pumps would feed them, leaving fewer parts to fail. It would stay with the capsule until the burn for home was done, then be cast off before reentry.

gemini-direct-ascent-craft.name: Gemini Direct Ascent spacecraft
gemini-direct-ascent-craft.description: A Gemini capsule stacked on landing and ascent modules, all landing on the Moon together.
gemini-direct-ascent-craft.historyNote: McDonnell's direct-ascent Gemini would have braked toward the Moon with a module built around the RL10, the hydrogen-burning engine of the Centaur stage. The RL10 first flew on 27 November 1963, the first hydrogen engine to fire in space. Versions of it are still flying today, on upper stages of rockets that launch satellites and probes.
gemini-direct-ascent-craft.longDescription: A stack of four parts, launched whole on a single heavy rocket. A retrograde module with an RL10 engine handled the coast to the Moon and most of the braking, then was dropped before touchdown; a terminal landing module took the craft the rest of the way down. After about a day on the surface, a service module lifted the crew off and fired them home, leaving only a Gemini reentry module, rebuilt for the speed of a lunar return, to come down through the air.

gemini-eor-service-module.name: Gemini EOR service module
gemini-eor-service-module.description: A service module for the lunar trip, joined to the capsule in Earth orbit.
gemini-eor-service-module.historyNote: Gemini's real service section stayed in orbit: everything that didn't need to come home, the thrusters, the propellant, the oxygen, the power, was packed in an adapter behind the capsule and discarded before reentry. Gemini 5 in 1965 was the first to carry fuel cells there, making electricity from hydrogen and oxygen, with water as the byproduct, for an eight-day flight.
gemini-eor-service-module.longDescription: Gemini's own adapter came in two parts: a retrograde section with four solid rockets that fired one after another to leave orbit, and an equipment section with 16 small thrusters for moving and turning, their propellant, and the life support. Joined to the capsule in Earth orbit, a service module for the Moon stretches the same idea to a trip of a week or more: bigger tanks, more oxygen and water, and enough thrust to correct the course on the way there and back.

langley-lunar-lander.name: Langley light lunar lander
langley-lunar-lander.description: A minimal open lander for one astronaut in a spacesuit: little more than an engine, tanks and a platform to stand on.
langley-lunar-lander.historyNote: NASA Langley's lander idea of 1961 was never built, but Langley built the next best thing: a steel gantry about 70 meters tall that held up five-sixths of a full-size lander's weight on cables. Twenty-four Apollo astronauts practiced the last 150 feet of a lunar landing there. Asked what landing on the Moon was like, Neil Armstrong said: like Langley.
langley-lunar-lander.longDescription: The Langley lander was a design for the least a Moon landing could need: a rocket engine, propellant tanks, landing legs and a platform for one astronaut to stand on in his suit, with no pressurized cabin at all. Leaving out the cabin saved its walls, its air and the systems to keep it, and kept the craft to a few tonnes fully fueled: about 4.4 t with storable propellants, less with hydrogen and oxygen. The suit was the astronaut's only shelter all the way down and back.

s-ivb-space-tug.name: S-IVB Space Tug
s-ivb-space-tug.description: A Saturn upper stage used as a tug in Earth orbit, pushing the assembled craft out toward the Moon.
s-ivb-space-tug.historyNote: From Apollo 13 on, the spent S-IVB stage wasn't sent off into orbit around the Sun but steered into the Moon. Apollo 13's stage hit at about 2.6 km/s on 15 April 1970, about 135 km from the seismometer Apollo 12 had left behind. The shaking it recorded helped work out what lies under the Moon's surface. Its crater is about 30 meters across.
s-ivb-space-tug.longDescription: The S-IVB was the Saturn V's third stage: about 17.8 m long and 6.6 m across, with one J-2 engine of about 1,000 kN burning liquid hydrogen and oxygen. Unlike most stages it could shut down and start again, so it could finish the climb to orbit and later, after a coast, fire again for the Moon in a burn of nearly six minutes. As a tug it makes that second burn for a stack assembled in Earth orbit, which means keeping its hydrogen cold while the pieces come together.

apollo-csm.name: Apollo command and service module
apollo-csm.description: The three-person command module and the service module behind it, whose engine brakes into lunar orbit and brings the crew home.
apollo-csm.historyNote: The engine that brought Apollo home from the Moon had to work. So it was as simple as an engine can be: fed by gas pressure instead of pumps, with fuel and oxidizer that ignite on contact, so it needed no igniter. Its valves, plumbing and electronics were doubled; only the combustion chamber and nozzle had no backup.
apollo-csm.longDescription: The command module was a cone 3.9 m across and 3.65 m tall, with about 6 m³ for three people. The service module behind it, a 7.6 m cylinder, held the 91 kN main engine, its propellant and the fuel cells. Together they weighed about 29 t. Returning at about 11 km/s, it flew blunt end first with its center of mass offset to make a little lift, and rolling it steered the descent. Its ablative heat shield, 2 to 7 cm thick, charred away, and three parachutes set it down.

apollo-lunar-module.name: Apollo lunar module
apollo-lunar-module.description: A two-stage lander: the descent stage stays on the Moon as a launch pad, the ascent stage flies the crew back to orbit.
apollo-lunar-module.historyNote: Grumman fought the lunar module's weight from the first drawing. The seats went, so the crew flew standing, held by harnesses, which let the windows shrink because the astronauts' eyes were closer to them. In places the pressurized cabin's wall was about 0.3 mm thick, a few layers of kitchen foil, wrapped in insulation and a thin outer skin.
apollo-lunar-module.longDescription: Fully loaded, the lunar module weighed about 15 t, more than half of it propellant. The descent stage, an octagonal frame 4.2 m across on four legs spanning 9.4 m, carried an engine of about 45 kN that could be throttled far down for the slow final approach, while crushable aluminum honeycomb in the legs absorbed the touchdown. The ascent stage had a fixed engine of about 16 kN and lifted off from the descent stage, which stayed behind as its launch pad.

soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.name: Soyuz 7K-L1 spacecraft
soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.description: A Soyuz without its orbital module, to save weight for the trip around the Moon.
soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.historyNote: On its way back from the Moon in November 1968, Zond 6 lost its cabin air through a faulty seal, and its parachute was released too high. It crashed in Kazakhstan, and engineers had to dig its film out of the wreck; the far-side photographs were published anyway. A crew aboard would not have survived, and Apollo 8 flew around the Moon the next month.
soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.longDescription: The 7K-L1 kept the Soyuz descent and service modules, but in place of the orbital module it had a light support cone, saving weight. A dish antenna was added for the radio link from lunar distance, with star sensors and a gyroscope platform to navigate, and the reserve parachute was removed. To come home from the Moon it could skip off the upper air and dive in a second time, easing the load on a crew and landing in Kazakhstan instead of the Indian Ocean.

soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.name: Soyuz 7K-LOK spacecraft
soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.description: A Soyuz built for lunar orbit, with a bigger engine and a docking system for the LK lander.
soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.historyNote: The lunar Soyuz, the 7K-LOK, flew only on top of an N1. On 23 November 1972 the fourth N1 lifted off with an uncrewed LOK and a dummy LK aboard for a test around the Moon. After 107 seconds, just before its first stage was due to finish, an engine exploded. The launch escape system pulled the spacecraft clear. It was the last N1 ever launched.
soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.longDescription: The LOK was a Soyuz stretched for the Moon, about 10 m long and 9.85 t. Behind the descent module sat its own rocket stage: a main engine of about 33 kN for the 1,100 m/s burn home, and a smaller engine for adjustments in lunar orbit. Fuel cells replaced the solar panels, and their water went to the crew. On the orbital module's nose, a docking probe and a small window dome let the pilot dock with the LK by eye.

lk-lander.name: LK lander
lk-lander.description: A one-person lunar lander whose own engine block both finishes the landing and lifts it off again.
lk-lander.historyNote: Apollo's lunar module had two stages, one to land and one to take off. The LK used the same rocket unit for both, with a main engine and a backup beside it, because a failure on liftoff would strand the cosmonaut for good. A separate braking stage did most of the slowing and dropped away about 4 km above the surface.
lk-lander.longDescription: The LK stood about 5.2 m tall and weighed about 5.5 t, little more than a third of Apollo's lunar module. Its four landing legs stayed on the Moon as the launch stand. The cosmonaut flew it standing at a window, steering with a finger controller because the suit's arms moved poorly, with perhaps 20 seconds of hover to pick his spot. On top, a hexagonal grid with 108 sockets caught the docking probe of the lunar Soyuz.

soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.name: Soyuz 7K-OK spacecraft
soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.description: The Earth-orbit Soyuz: a descent module, an orbital module for living space, and a service module.
soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.historyNote: Vostok's ball fell through the air ballistically, with eight g or more on the pilot. Soyuz's bell-shaped descent capsule carries its weight off-center, so it flies tilted and makes a little lift, and turning it steers the landing and spreads the braking over a longer path: about four g on a normal return. In an emergency it spins to cancel the lift and falls straight in, at higher g.
soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.longDescription: The 7K-OK weighed about 6.5 t and was about 8 m long, its solar panels spanning nearly 10 m. At the front, the round orbital module gave room to work and sleep and carried the docking unit: a probe on the active ship, a cone on the passive one, with no hatch through it, so crews crossed between docked ships outside. The bell-shaped descent module held the crew for launch and landing, and the service module at the back carried the engine and its propellant.

igla-docking-system.name: Igla docking system
igla-docking-system.description: Radar antennas and electronics that let two Soyuz craft find each other and dock with nobody steering.
igla-docking-system.historyNote: Igla, Russian for needle, measured direction and distance to its target by comparing radio signals across several antennas. It needed the target to help: the station or craft being approached had to turn its docking port toward the newcomer and keep it there. For large stations that cost too much fuel, so in the 1980s Igla gave way to Kurs.
igla-docking-system.longDescription: Igla needed antennas on both craft. On the active ship, one set searched for the target, a gyro-stabilized set then locked on and tracked it, and a third set guided the final approach. From their signals the system worked out range, closing speed and direction, and fired the engines to bring the ships together slowly, aligned to about a degree, until the probe of one met the cone of the other.

lk-700-spacecraft.name: LK-700 spacecraft
lk-700-spacecraft.description: A heavy lunar craft built to land and take off again in one piece, with no rendezvous in lunar orbit.
lk-700-spacecraft.historyNote: The LK-700 grew out of Vladimir Chelomei's LK-1, a two-seat craft for flying around the Moon on his Proton rocket. In 1965 the government took the flyby from him and gave it to Korolev, whose Soyuz 7K-L1 flew instead. Chelomei turned to landing, and presented the direct-ascent LK-700 to an expert commission in November 1966.
lk-700-spacecraft.longDescription: In Chelomei's design the LK-700 was one craft for the whole trip, with no lander to meet in lunar orbit: a stack of rocket stages under a capsule. A landing stage of about 3.5 t on six legs set it down, on slopes of up to 15 degrees. The return stage, about 11.7 t, then lifted off and fired for Earth, leaving only the landing stage behind. The capsule, an Apollo-like cone of about 3.1 t, flew slightly tilted to make lift and steer its landing.

gemini-eva-suit.name: Gemini spacesuit
gemini-eva-suit.description: A pressure suit with an umbilical hose for oxygen and a tether, for work outside the capsule.
gemini-eva-suit.historyNote: On Gemini 9A in June 1966 Gene Cernan was to strap on a rocket backpack at the rear of the spacecraft. With nothing to brace against, every move took far more effort than expected; his heart rate climbed to about 180 and his breath fogged his visor from the inside. The backpack test was called off. Better cooling, foot restraints, handholds and underwater training followed.
gemini-eva-suit.longDescription: The suit was built up in layers: a rubberized nylon bladder holding oxygen at about 0.26 bar, a link net to stop it ballooning out of shape, and an outer cover. Suits for work outside added layers of Mylar insulation and protection against micrometeoroids. An umbilical hose from the capsule supplied oxygen, with a tether to keep the wearer from drifting off; later flights added a chest pack to regulate the flow. Ed White first wore one outside in June 1965.

apollo-lunar-eva-suit.name: Apollo lunar surface suit
apollo-lunar-eva-suit.description: A suit with its own backpack for oxygen and cooling, built for hours of walking on the Moon.
apollo-lunar-eva-suit.historyNote: Apollo's moon suits came from ILC, the company behind Playtex bras and girdles, and the women who sewed them came from its Playtex sewing floor. Each suit was made by hand to fit one astronaut, from about 21 layers, some glued and some stitched, with seams that had to be accurate to the width of a pin.
apollo-lunar-eva-suit.longDescription: The lunar suit was a rubberized pressure garment inside a multilayer outer cover against heat, cold and micrometeoroids, held at about 25 kPa of pure oxygen. Underneath, a mesh garment laced with tubes carried cooling water. The backpack supplied oxygen, cooling and radio for about 6 hours, 7 on the last three missions, whose suits also gained a waist joint so the astronauts could sit on the rover. With the backpack it weighed about 91 kg on Earth, about 15 kg on the Moon.

light-lunar-eva-suit.name: Light lunar suit
light-lunar-eva-suit.description: A lighter surface suit for the open Langley lander, where the suit is the crew's only cabin.
light-lunar-eva-suit.historyNote: How do you cool an astronaut in a vacuum? Apollo's life-support backpack pumped cold water through tubes in a garment worn under the suit, then past a metal plate full of tiny pores with vacuum on the far side. Water seeping through the plate froze, and the ice turned straight to vapor, carrying the body's heat away. The more heat, the faster the ice went.
light-lunar-eva-suit.longDescription: With no cabin around the astronaut, the suit had to do everything a cabin does: hold pressure, supply oxygen, remove carbon dioxide and body heat, and shield against the Sun's glare and the cold of shadow. Gemini's spacewalks showed how hard that was: on Gemini 9A in June 1966 Gene Cernan overheated and his visor fogged until he could barely see. A light suit for the open lander needs its own life-support pack and still has to bend enough to climb aboard.

lunar-roving-vehicle.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle
lunar-roving-vehicle.description: A folding electric car for two astronauts, carried on the lunar module's side.
lunar-roving-vehicle.historyNote: On Apollo 17's first moonwalk Gene Cernan caught a rover fender with a hammer and tore part of it off, and the wheels began throwing up plumes of dark dust. Overnight, engineers on the ground worked out a fix: next morning the crew taped four spare maps together into a new fender and fixed it in place with two clamps borrowed from the lunar module's lights.
lunar-roving-vehicle.longDescription: The rover was a 210 kg aluminum-frame car 3.1 m long that could carry about 490 kg, more than twice its own weight. Each wheel had its own small electric motor, fed by two 36 V silver-zinc batteries, and a tire of woven steel wire with titanium treads. It rode folded against the lunar module's side and unfolded as the crew lowered it on tapes. A gyro and the wheels' odometers kept track of the way back, and drives were planned to stay within walking distance of the lander.

berkut-eva-suit.name: Berkut spacesuit
berkut-eva-suit.description: A Soviet pressure suit with a backpack of oxygen, made for the first walk outside a spacecraft.
berkut-eva-suit.historyNote: Leonov's Berkut suit was white rather than the orange of earlier Soviet suits, so it would reflect sunlight, and it carried 30 to 45 minutes of oxygen in a backpack. It ran at 0.4 atmospheres, a compromise between enough pressure to breathe and a suit soft enough to bend.
berkut-eva-suit.longDescription: The Berkut was a modified SK-1, the Vostok pilots' suit, made by the Zvezda plant. Its pressure shell had three layers, a main and a backup airtight layer inside a load-bearing outer one, all under a cover of vacuum insulation. Oxygen from bottles in the backpack flowed through the helmet and suit and was then vented into space. A switch set the pressure to one of two levels, 0.4 atmospheres or a softer 0.27. Suit and backpack together weighed about 41 kg.

yastreb-eva-suit.name: Yastreb spacesuit
yastreb-eva-suit.description: A suit for spacewalks between two docked Soyuz craft.
yastreb-eva-suit.historyNote: The Yastreb carried its life support in a white metal box on the chest and stomach rather than on the back, so it would fit through Soyuz's narrow hatches. Two cosmonauts wore it in January 1969 to cross from Soyuz 5 to Soyuz 4 on the outside. Nobody filmed the crossing: the camera that was meant to record it was never set up.
yastreb-eva-suit.longDescription: Yastreb was a suit for spacewalks between docked Soyuz craft, designed at Zvezda in 1966 after Alexei Leonov's Berkut suit had ballooned so stiff in vacuum that he struggled to get back into Voskhod 2. Yastreb's joints used pulleys and cables to keep their shape under pressure. The suit alone weighed about 20 kg and its life-support box about 21 kg, enough for about two and a half hours outside. It was used on one mission only.

krechet-eva-suit.name: Krechet lunar suit
krechet-eva-suit.description: A semi-rigid lunar suit entered through a hatch in its back.
krechet-eva-suit.historyNote: A cosmonaut landing alone on the Moon would have nobody to help with the zips. So the Krechet lunar suit was entered through a door in its back, with the backpack built into the door, and closed with a lever by the right elbow. The idea outlived the Moon program: the Orlan suits Russian cosmonauts still use for spacewalks open the same way.
krechet-eva-suit.longDescription: The Krechet, entered from the back, was the first semi-rigid suit: a hard upper torso of aluminum alloy with soft fabric arms and legs, ball-bearing joints at the shoulders and wrists, and joints at the waist and hips for bending down. A control panel folded down from the chest. Its life support lasted about 10 hours between refills, and a ring on the back let a fallen cosmonaut roll onto his side and stand. It weighed about 106 kg on Earth, under 18 kg on the Moon.

r7-voskhod.name: R-7 (Voskhod)
r7-voskhod.description: The R-7 with a more powerful upper stage, able to lift the heavier Voskhod.
r7-voskhod.historyNote: The Voskhod rocket, the R-7 with a bigger third stage, flew about 300 times between 1963 and 1976. Only two of those launches carried people. Many of the rest put Zenit reconnaissance satellites into orbit, spy satellites whose cameras and film came back to Earth in a capsule. Its busiest year, 1969, saw 32 flights.

r7-luna.name: R-7 (Luna)
r7-luna.description: The R-7 with a small third stage that sends probes to the Moon.
r7-luna.historyNote: Luna 1 left on 2 January 1959, on the first R-7 with a third stage that worked. The next day, about 113,000 km out, it released a kilogram of sodium vapor, a glowing artificial comet that observers photographed from the ground to check its path. It was aimed at the Moon, missed by about 6,000 km because of an error in the engine's cutoff, and became the first spacecraft to orbit the Sun.

r7-molniya.name: R-7 (Molniya)
r7-molniya.description: The R-7 with a stage that restarts in orbit, for flights to the Moon and the planets.
r7-molniya.historyNote: The R-7 with a fourth stage was named after its most famous payload: Molniya, Russian for lightning, the first Soviet communications satellites. They flew a long 12-hour orbit tilted at 63.4 degrees, at which the orbit's high point doesn't drift. Each satellite hung for hours high over the far north, where satellites over the equator are hard to see from, and three of them covered it around the clock.

r7-soyuz.name: R-7 (Soyuz)
r7-soyuz.description: The R-7 version built for the Soyuz spacecraft, with an escape tower for the crew.
r7-soyuz.historyNote: The R-7 began as the world's first intercontinental missile in the 1950s, and it was soon too big and slow to be a good one. As a launcher it never retired: its Soyuz descendants still carry crews into orbit today. Counting every version, the family has flown more than 1,900 times, more than any other rocket in history.

proton.name: Proton
proton.description: A heavy rocket on storable propellants, powerful enough for the largest probes.
proton.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei designed the UR-500 as a missile to carry an enormous nuclear warhead. It never served as one. Its first flights, from July 1965, carried Proton, a series of heavy satellites of over 12 tonnes for studying cosmic rays, and the rocket took their name. Modern versions of it were still flying more than half a century later.

proton-k-block-d.name: Proton-K with Block D
proton-k-block-d.description: The Proton with a restartable upper stage, able to send a crewed craft around the Moon.
proton-k-block-d.historyNote: The Block D stage was built for the Soviet Moon landing: as the N1's fifth stage it would correct the course to the Moon, brake into lunar orbit and start the LK's descent. On top of a Proton it found a longer life, sending Zond capsules around the Moon, and Luna 16, Lunokhod, Mars 3 and Venera 9 on their way. A later version first took Soviet satellites to geostationary orbit.

n1.name: N1
n1.description: The giant Soviet Moon rocket, its first stage driven by a ring of many smaller engines.
n1.historyNote: The N1's first stage had 30 engines, more than any rocket before it. A control system called KORD watched them, and if one failed it shut down the one opposite to keep the thrust balanced. All four launches failed. On the second, on 3 July 1969, an oxygen pump exploded as it lifted off, and the rocket fell back onto the pad, and the pad took about 18 months to rebuild.

ur-700.name: UR-700
ur-700.description: A proposed giant rocket for a direct flight to the Moon, built from storable-propellant modules.
ur-700.historyNote: Chelomei's UR-700 was a bundle of rocket modules with one big engine each: six around the outside as the first stage and three in the middle as the second, nine engines in all, carrying about 150 tonnes to low orbit. Its RD-270 engine, by Valentin Glushko's bureau, was test-fired 27 times between 1967 and 1969, but the rocket was never built.

juno-2.name: Juno II
juno-2.description: A Jupiter missile with small solid upper stages, for probes to the Moon and beyond.
juno-2.historyNote: The Juno II was a Jupiter missile with stretched tanks, a stronger frame for the upper stages and radio guidance from the ground, topped with clusters of small solid rockets. It had a rough record: six of its ten launches failed. Pioneer 4 in March 1959 was a success, and so was Explorer 7 in October 1959, which made the first measurements of the energy the Earth gains from the Sun and gives off.

thor-able.name: Thor-Able
thor-able.description: A Thor missile with an upper stage on top: an early workhorse for small satellites and probes.
thor-able.historyNote: On 14 August 1959 Explorer 6, launched a week earlier on a Thor-Able, sent back the first picture of the Earth from orbit. Its camera was a simple scanning eye that swept the view in strips as the satellite spun, and engineers pieced the strips together like a shredded letter. The blurry result showed sunlit clouds over the Pacific, the first step toward weather satellites.

atlas-agena.name: Atlas-Agena
atlas-agena.description: An Atlas with the restartable Agena upper stage, for lunar and planetary probes.
atlas-agena.historyNote: On 22 July 1962 an Atlas-Agena carrying Mariner 1 to Venus veered off course and was destroyed. A symbol in the guidance equations had lost its bar, the mark meaning a smoothed average, so the software chased noise as if it were real drift. The press called it the most expensive hyphen in history. Five weeks later Mariner 2 left for Venus, and it made the first flyby of another planet in December.

atlas-centaur.name: Atlas-Centaur
atlas-centaur.description: An Atlas with the Centaur, the first upper stage burning liquid hydrogen, for heavier probes.
atlas-centaur.historyNote: The first Atlas-Centaur, in May 1962, broke up less than a minute after launch when insulation panels on the hydrogen tank failed. Wernher von Braun recommended cancelling the stage, and in November President Kennedy suggested the same. It survived because Surveyor depended on it, and because Apollo needed experience with liquid hydrogen. In 1966 it sent Surveyor 1 to its landing on the Moon.

titan-2.name: Titan II
titan-2.description: A missile on storable propellants, made human-rated to fly the Gemini capsule.
titan-2.historyNote: The Titan II was a missile, and it shook: a vibration along its length that the Air Force could live with was far beyond what NASA would accept for astronauts, a quarter of a g. A first fix made it worse, doubling the shaking. Then engineers found the cause, bubbles forming at the pump inlets, and gas-filled dampers in the feed lines brought it down to about a tenth of a g.

titan-3c.name: Titan IIIC
titan-3c.description: A Titan with two large solid boosters strapped to its sides and a Transtage on top.
titan-3c.historyNote: The Titan IIIC lifted off on its two big solid boosters alone, each three meters wide and built from five segments stacked near the pad. The liquid-fuelled core in the middle only lit high in the air, as the solids' thrust tailed off. At its first flight in 1965 it was the most powerful rocket that had ever flown.

titan-3e-centaur.name: Titan IIIE-Centaur
titan-3e-centaur.description: A Titan with solid boosters and a Centaur on top, for the outer planets.
titan-3e-centaur.historyNote: The first Titan IIIE-Centaur, in February 1974, failed when its Centaur stage did not ignite. It flew six more times and never failed again, and those six flights launched some of the most famous probes there are: Helios 1 and 2 toward the Sun, Viking 1 and 2 to Mars, and Voyager 2 and Voyager 1 to the outer planets.

saturn-1.name: Saturn I
saturn-1.description: The first Saturn, its first stage a cluster of eight engines fed from a cluster of tanks.
saturn-1.historyNote: The Saturn I's first stage was a bundle: eight narrow tanks around one wide one, all at the diameters of the Redstone and Jupiter missiles so their tooling could be used, feeding eight engines. Skeptics called it Cluster's Last Stand. It flew ten times without a failure, launched the three Pegasus satellites and flew test versions of the Apollo spacecraft.

saturn-1b.name: Saturn IB
saturn-1b.description: An improved Saturn I with a hydrogen upper stage, able to put an Apollo into Earth orbit.
saturn-1b.historyNote: The Saturn IB was much shorter than the Saturn V, but the launch pads at the Kennedy Space Center had been built for the giant. So NASA stood it on a pedestal about 39 meters tall, nicknamed the milkstool, until its upper stage and spacecraft lined up with the service arms. It launched the three Skylab crews from it in 1973.

saturn-c3b.name: Saturn C-3B
saturn-c3b.description: A Saturn design between the IB and the V, for lunar missions assembled in Earth orbit.
saturn-c3b.historyNote: The C in the early Saturn names wasn't an abbreviation: the designs were options lettered A, B and C, and Saturn C was chosen and numbered. The C-1 became the Saturn I and the C-5 the Saturn V. The C-3 never flew: it would have used two of the Saturn V's big engines, and Marshall planned to build a Moon ship from several of them in Earth orbit.

saturn-v.name: Saturn V
saturn-v.description: The three-stage giant that sends a complete Apollo spacecraft to the Moon.
saturn-v.historyNote: The Saturn V's F-1 engines suffered from combustion instability: pressure waves sloshing across the combustion chamber could tear an engine apart within moments. Engineers added copper baffles across the injector plate, then tested them the hard way, setting off small bombs inside running engines to see whether the baffles would calm the disturbance. It took more than 1,300 test firings.

nova.name: Nova
nova.description: The giant that was never built: eight F-1 engines, big enough to land a whole spacecraft on the Moon and fly it home.
nova.historyNote: Direct ascent, landing the whole spacecraft and flying it home, needed a rocket far bigger than the Saturn V. NASA's Nova studies drew one with eight F-1 engines in its first stage, able to send about 68 tonnes toward the Moon. It was never built: lunar-orbit rendezvous needed only a small lander, so the Saturn V was enough, and the factory at Michoud was too low for a stage that wide.

sputnik-1-orbit.name: Orbital flight
sputnik-1-orbit.description: Launch the satellite and keep it transmitting from orbit for a season.

sputnik-1-extended.name: Extended mission
sputnik-1-extended.description: A longer flight with more battery capacity, spread over three seasons, for more science and more prestige. Sputnik 1 never flew one: this is what a next step could have looked like.

sputnik-2-orbit.name: Orbital flight with a dog
sputnik-2-orbit.description: Put the cabin and its passenger into orbit and send back the dog's heartbeat and breathing. There is no return.

korabl-sputnik-2-orbit.name: Biological flight and recovery
korabl-sputnik-2-orbit.description: A day in orbit with a cabin full of animals and plants, then retrofire, reentry and a landing on home territory with everything alive.

11-descent-and-splashdown.name: Descent and landing
11-descent-and-splashdown.description: Parachutes bring the capsule down on home territory, where the recovery team gets the animals out and back to the doctors.

vostok-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
vostok-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Try out the capsule on a short up-and-down flight, with a mannequin in the seat, before risking a pilot. The real program skipped this step: the R-7 was built for orbit.

08-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

vostok-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
vostok-suborbital.description: A pilot's first ride: about a quarter of an hour on a ballistic arc with a few minutes of weightlessness, then an ejection and a parachute landing.

07-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

vostok-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
vostok-uncrewed-orbital.description: One full orbit with nobody aboard, flown by the automatics and brought down on command from the ground. A mannequin in the seat tests the ejection.
vostok-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: The 'pilot' of the last two test flights, in March 1961, was a mannequin called Ivan Ivanovich, the Russian 'John Doe'. To test the radio without starting rumors of a secret cosmonaut, his voice channel played a recording of a choir and of a man reading out a recipe for borscht.

vostok-orbital.name: Orbital flight
vostok-orbital.description: The real thing: a cosmonaut aboard for at least one full orbit, then retrofire, reentry and ejection over home ground.
vostok-orbital.historyNote: Nobody knew whether a person could still think clearly in weightlessness, so Vostok 1's manual controls were locked. The unlock code, 1-2-5, was sealed in an envelope on board, on the theory that anyone able to enter it was fit to fly. Several people simply told Gagarin the code before launch.

vostok-orbital-duration-1.name: Day-long orbital flight
vostok-orbital-duration-1.description: Stay up for a full day or more and show that a person can eat, sleep and work in weightlessness.
vostok-orbital-duration-1.historyNote: In August 1961 Gherman Titov spent just over a day in orbit on Vostok 2. He was the first person to sleep in space, and the first to suffer from space sickness, which worried the doctors enough to shape the following flights.

vostok-orbital-duration-2.name: Multi-day orbital flight
vostok-orbital-duration-2.description: Several days in orbit, as long as the capsule's supplies allow, with the cosmonaut's health watched the whole time.
vostok-orbital-duration-2.historyNote: Valery Bykovsky's Vostok 5, in June 1963, stayed up for almost five days. It is still the longest spaceflight anyone has made alone. Two days into his flight, Valentina Tereshkova launched on Vostok 6 and became the first woman in space.

vostok-joint-orbital.name: Group flight
vostok-joint-orbital.description: Launch two capsules a day apart into almost the same orbit, so that they pass close enough to talk by radio.
vostok-joint-orbital.historyNote: In August 1962 Vostok 3 and 4 came within about 6.5 km of each other, and the press spoke of a rendezvous. It wasn't one: neither capsule could change its orbit, the second launch was simply timed perfectly, and the two drifted apart. Real rendezvous is counterintuitive: to catch a craft ahead of you, you first slow down, which drops you to a lower, faster orbit.

explorer-1-orbit.name: Orbital flight
explorer-1-orbit.description: Launch the satellite and send back what its instruments find, for a season.
explorer-1-orbit.historyNote: Explorer 1 carried no tape recorder. Its counts went out live by radio and reached the Earth only while it passed within range of a ground station, a few minutes at a time, so its record of each orbit was full of gaps. Its radio kept going until 23 May 1958; the satellite itself stayed in orbit until 31 March 1970.

explorer-1-extended.name: Extended mission
explorer-1-extended.description: A longer flight with more battery capacity, spread over three seasons, for more science and more prestige. Explorer 1 never flew one: this is what a next step could have looked like.

mercury-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
mercury-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the capsule on a short arc without an astronaut, to prove the rocket, the escape system and the recovery at sea.
mercury-uncrewed-suborbital.historyNote: In January 1961, ahead of Alan Shepard, a chimpanzee named Ham rode the capsule. He pulled levers in answer to lights during the flight, showing that work was possible in weightlessness. His capsule came down far off target and began taking on water before the recovery helicopter reached it.

07-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

mercury-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
mercury-suborbital.description: About fifteen minutes on a ballistic arc: launch, a few minutes of weightlessness, and a splashdown far downrange.
mercury-suborbital.historyNote: In July 1961, moments after splashdown, Liberty Bell 7's hatch blew off. Gus Grissom swam out as the capsule filled and sank. It lay on the floor of the Atlantic, nearly 5 km down, until an expedition raised it in 1999.

07-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

mercury-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
mercury-uncrewed-orbital.description: Send the capsule around the Earth with no astronaut aboard, to prove its life support and controls before risking a crew.
mercury-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: In November 1961 a chimpanzee named Enos flew two orbits in a Mercury capsule. The flight was cut short by a stuck thruster and an overheating suit system, problems that were fixed before John Glenn flew the same mission three months later.

mercury-orbital.name: Orbital flight
mercury-orbital.description: An astronaut aboard for a few orbits, then retrofire, reentry and splashdown where the recovery ships wait.
mercury-orbital.historyNote: Scott Carpenter's Aurora 7, in May 1962, came down about 400 km past its target. The capsule was misaligned when the retrorockets fired, and they fired a few seconds late. He waited in his life raft for about three hours before a helicopter lifted him out.

mercury-orbital-duration-1.name: Day-long orbital flight
mercury-orbital-duration-1.description: A day or more in orbit, to learn how a person copes with weightlessness over a whole day of work and sleep.
mercury-orbital-duration-1.historyNote: Gordon Cooper's Faith 7, in May 1963, flew 22 orbits in about 34 hours. Near the end, a short circuit knocked out the automatic controls. Cooper lined the capsule up using lines drawn on his window, timed the retrofire with his wristwatch, and flew the reentry by hand, splashing down a few kilometers from the recovery ship.

mercury-joint-orbital.name: Joint launch
mercury-joint-orbital.description: Two capsules launched close together into neighboring orbits. Mercury never flew this: it points toward the rendezvous flights that came next.

pegasus-orbit.name: Orbital flight
pegasus-orbit.description: Unfold the panels in orbit and count micrometeoroid hits for a season.

pegasus-extended.name: Extended mission
pegasus-extended.description: Keep counting impacts for several seasons, for a far better estimate of the risk.

biosatellite-orbit.name: Orbital flight
biosatellite-orbit.description: Fly the organisms in orbit and recover the capsule with them.

biosatellite-extended.name: Extended mission
biosatellite-extended.description: A longer stay in orbit before recovery, to see how the organisms develop over time.

orbiting-frog-otolith-orbit.name: Orbital flight
orbiting-frog-otolith-orbit.description: Record the frogs' balance organs as they adjust to weightlessness.

orbiting-frog-otolith-extended.name: Extended mission
orbiting-frog-otolith-extended.description: Keep recording for longer, to see whether the frogs' sense of balance settles.

pioneer-4-flyby.name: Lunar flyby
pioneer-4-flyby.description: Fly past the Moon, measuring radiation on the way, and on into orbit around the Sun.

zond-5-flyby.name: Lunar flyby with animals
zond-5-flyby.description: Send the uncrewed capsule around the Moon and bring its passengers home through the atmosphere at lunar return speed.

ranger-3-impact.name: Lunar impact
ranger-3-impact.description: Aim the probe at the Moon and send pictures until it strikes.

luna-2-impact.name: Lunar impact
luna-2-impact.description: Hit the Moon: reaching another world, even by crashing into it.

pioneer-2-orbit.name: Lunar orbit
pioneer-2-orbit.description: Fire the probe's own motor to brake into orbit around the Moon.

lunar-orbiter-mapping.name: Lunar mapping
lunar-orbiter-mapping.description: Photograph the Moon from orbit to find safe landing sites.

surveyor-landing.name: Soft landing
surveyor-landing.description: Land gently on the Moon and photograph and probe the ground around the lander.

luna-15-sample-return.name: Sample return
luna-15-sample-return.description: Land, drill into the surface, and launch the sample back to Earth in a sealed capsule.
luna-15-sample-return.historyNote: Luna 15 and Luna 16 were the same machine, the Ye-8-5: a landing stage with a drill arm, carrying a small ascent rocket with the sealed return capsule on top. To save weight, the designers took one of the ascent stage's two radio transmitters out of Luna 15 before launch, leaving the whole trip home with no spare.

luna-3-flyby.name: Far side flyby
luna-3-flyby.description: Loop around the Moon and photograph the side the Earth never sees.

luna-17-landing.name: Landing with a rover
luna-17-landing.description: Land and drive the rover off its ramps to explore the surface by remote control.

pioneer-sun-orbit.name: Solar orbit
pioneer-sun-orbit.description: Leave the Earth behind and measure the solar wind from an orbit around the Sun.

mariner-10-flyby.name: Venus and Mercury flyby
mariner-10-flyby.description: Swing past Venus and use its gravity to reach Mercury.

mariner-5-flyby.name: Venus flyby
mariner-5-flyby.description: Fly close past Venus and measure its atmosphere.

pioneer-venus-orbit.name: Venus orbit
pioneer-venus-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Venus and map it by radar.

venera-15-orbit.name: Venus orbit
venera-15-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Venus and map its surface by radar.

pioneer-venus-multiprobe-entry.name: Atmospheric probes
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-entry.description: Release the probes ahead of arrival and let them fall through Venus's atmosphere at four different points.

venera-7-landing.name: Venus landing
venera-7-landing.description: Send the capsule down through Venus's atmosphere and keep it talking from the surface.

venera-flyby-and-lander.name: Flyby and lander
venera-flyby-and-lander.description: The carrier flies past Venus and relays the lander's signal while the lander goes down.
venera-flyby-and-lander.historyNote: Venera 13 landed on 1 March 1982 and sent back the first color pictures from the surface of Venus: flat, slabby rocks and soil under an orange sky. It was built to last 32 minutes on the surface and kept working for 127, a record no other lander on Venus has beaten.

venera-orbiter-and-lander.name: Orbiter and lander
venera-orbiter-and-lander.description: The carrier brakes into orbit and relays the lander's signal from the surface.
venera-orbiter-and-lander.historyNote: On the way to Venus the lander rode inside a sphere 2.4 meters across, its heat shield. In the upper air the sphere came off in halves as the parachutes opened, and the lander hung under its main canopies for about 20 minutes before dropping them. It touched down on a hollow metal ring around its base, built to crumple and soak up the blow.

mariner-6-flyby.name: Mars flyby
mariner-6-flyby.description: Fly past Mars and photograph its surface.

mariner-9-orbit.name: Mars orbit
mariner-9-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Mars and map the planet.

viking-orbiter-and-lander.name: Orbiter and lander
viking-orbiter-and-lander.description: Survey Mars from orbit, then land and test the soil for signs of life.

mars-2-orbiter-lander-rover.name: Orbiter, lander and rover
mars-2-orbiter-lander-rover.description: Brake into orbit, send the lander down, and walk the small rover across the surface.
mars-2-orbiter-lander-rover.historyNote: Mars 2 and Mars 3 let their landers go about four and a half hours out. Each lander was to spin itself up and fire a small solid rocket to set its angle into the atmosphere. Mars 2's last course correction was so accurate that nothing more was needed, but its computer, programmed to expect an error, turned the lander anyway. It came in far too steeply, its parachute never opened, and it crashed.

mars-m69-orbit.name: Mars orbit
mars-m69-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Mars and photograph the planet.

pioneer-10-flyby.name: Jupiter flyby
pioneer-10-flyby.description: Cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter.

pioneer-11-flyby.name: Jupiter and Saturn flyby
pioneer-11-flyby.description: Fly past Jupiter and use its gravity to reach Saturn.
pioneer-11-flyby.historyNote: Pioneer 11 was Pioneer 10's twin, with one more instrument, an extra magnetometer for the giant planets' strong fields. On the way out one of the booms carrying its nuclear generators was briefly slow to deploy, but nothing put the mission at risk. It passed Jupiter at 42,500 km, about three times closer than Pioneer 10.

x-15-flight-test.name: Flight test
x-15-flight-test.description: Drop from the carrier aircraft, light the engine and prove the plane flies, before pushing for speed and height.
x-15-flight-test.historyNote: Scott Crossfield flew the X-15 for the first time on 8 June 1959, released from under a B-52's wing to glide down to a dry lake bed with no rocket fuel aboard. Its first powered flight, on 17 September, used two smaller interim engines: the big engine built for it wasn't ready yet. Crossfield reached about Mach 2.1.

x-15-research-flight-1.name: Research flight: altitude
x-15-research-flight-1.description: Climb steeply to the edge of space, where the thrusters steer and the pilot sees the black sky.
x-15-research-flight-1.historyNote: The US Air Force gave astronaut wings for flights above 50 miles, about 80 km, and eight X-15 pilots earned them. The civilian pilots from NASA didn't get theirs until 2005. On 15 November 1967 Michael Adams went into a spin at about Mach 5 coming down from 81 km, and his X-15 broke up: the program's only fatal accident in 199 flights.

x-15-research-flight-2.name: Research flight: speed
x-15-research-flight-2.description: Hold a fast, level run at several times the speed of sound, where friction with the air heats the skin to hundreds of degrees.
x-15-research-flight-2.historyNote: For its speed record of Mach 6.7 in October 1967, the X-15A-2 was coated in a pink layer meant to char away and carried a dummy ramjet engine under its tail. Shock waves from the dummy heated the structure beside it beyond what the coating could take, burned holes in the skin, and tore the dummy away. The real ramjet never flew.

mig-e-154-drop-test.name: Drop test
mig-e-154-drop-test.description: Dropped from under the carrier's belly, light the engines and prove the plane flies, before pushing for height and speed.

gemini-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
gemini-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Gemini capsule without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.
gemini-uncrewed-suborbital.historyNote: Gemini 2's first launch attempt, on 9 December 1964, lasted one second: the engines lit and shut down again when a cracked valve cost hydraulic pressure and the rocket's malfunction detection switched to its backup. It flew on 19 January 1965, an 18-minute arc to test the heat shield, and was fished out of the Atlantic.

gemini-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
gemini-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Gemini capsule's first flight with people aboard.

gemini-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
gemini-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Gemini capsule into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.
gemini-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: Gemini 1, on 8 April 1964, was never meant to come home. The capsule stayed attached to its rocket's second stage, and engineers drilled four holes in its heat shield so it would be sure to burn up on reentry. Tracking stations followed it for four days until it came down over the South Atlantic.

gemini-orbital.name: Orbital flight
gemini-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Gemini capsule, and a safe return.
gemini-orbital.historyNote: Gemini 3, in March 1965, was the first American flight to change its own orbit. Gus Grissom named the capsule Molly Brown, after a musical about an unsinkable woman: his Mercury capsule had sunk. John Young smuggled a corned beef sandwich aboard. The crumbs could have fouled the electronics, and the crew were reprimanded.

gemini-spacewalk.name: Spacewalk (duration level I)
gemini-spacewalk.description: A longer flight in which one astronaut opens the hatch and goes outside on an umbilical.
gemini-spacewalk.historyNote: Ed White stepped out of Gemini 4 on 3 June 1965 with a small gas gun to push himself around. It ran dry after about three minutes, and he moved by tugging on his tether. Ordered back in as the spacecraft headed into darkness, he called it the saddest moment of his life. Then the hatch wouldn't latch, and the two of them fought it closed.

gemini-rendezvous.name: Rendezvous
gemini-rendezvous.description: Launch two Gemini capsules and steer one to within a few meters of the other.
gemini-rendezvous.historyNote: On 12 December 1965 Gemini 6A's engines lit and shut down after about a second and a half, with the rocket still on the pad. The rules said to eject. Wally Schirra judged that they hadn't lifted off and stayed put, which saved the spacecraft and the mission. Three days later they launched and caught Gemini 7.

gemini-docking.name: Docking
gemini-docking.description: Launch an Agena target, then a Gemini that finds it and docks.
gemini-docking.historyNote: Gemini 10, in July 1966, docked with its own Agena, used its engine to climb, and then went after a second target: the Agena left in orbit by Gemini 8 four months earlier. Michael Collins spacewalked across to it on a tether and retrieved a dust collector that had been waiting there since March, the first visit to another spacecraft in orbit.
